title: Role of the Business Analyst (vs Product/Project Manager)
one_screen: A BA in a bank translates business needs into requirements, focusing on *what* and *why*, unlike a product manager (who defines product strategy and features) or a project manager (who plans the *how* and *when* of delivery).
bodyText: Business Analysts (BAs) gather business requirements and ensure that solutions address true business needs. They act as the liaison between business stakeholders and technical teams. BAs **do not** own product strategy or delivery schedules. A *Product Manager* (or Product Owner) is outward-facing – they define the product vision, customer needs, and high-level features. A *Project Manager* is responsible for planning, coordinating, and tracking the project timeline, budget, and resources. In contrast, the BA identifies *what* must be done (the requirements) and *why* (the business objective), but generally not *how* to build it or *when* to schedule tasks. For example, if a regulator mandates a new report, the Product Manager ensures the business values it and fits into the roadmap, the Project Manager schedules the implementation, and the BA defines the report’s data requirements and rules. The BA does **not** decide how the report is coded or which team builds it, nor do they own the release date – those are the project manager’s concerns. ### Permanent rule A BA defines *what* needs to be done and *why*, but does **not** dictate the *how* (that’s the domain of solution architects or developers) or *when* (that’s the project manager’s schedule). ### Permanent trap Confusing the BA role with the project or product manager role. For instance, asking the BA to manage the project budget or delivery schedule, or to own product strategy, leads to failure. The BA must resist the urge to become a mini–project manager. ### Never confuse **Product Manager** — owns the product vision, market needs, and feature roadmap (external focus). --- **Project Manager** — owns the project plan, schedule, and budget (execution focus). ### No delta This distinction holds across jurisdictions: BAs globally focus on requirements gathering, whereas product/project management roles are organizational, not regulatory, differences.

title: Change Landscape: Regulatory vs Strategic vs Remediation
one_screen: Banks undertake strategic initiatives (growth or efficiency) and remediation (fixing defects), but *regulatory-driven* change is mandatory, with fixed deadlines and external oversight, requiring full compliance and auditability.
bodyText: Bank change programs fall into categories: **Strategic** (business-driven goals like new services or cost reduction), **Remediation** (fixing problems found by audit), and **Regulatory** (mandated by laws or regulators). Regulatory changes are unique: their deadlines are *unmovable* and non-negotiable, and failure to comply can incur penalties and license risk. These projects carry high visibility, involve many functions, and have huge impact. Because regulators require proof of compliance, regulatory programs demand rigorous documentation, traceability, and audit trails. For example, a compliance program like IFRS 9 transition is closely monitored by supervisors; banks often run parallel regimes to validate results before the fixed effective date. Strategic initiatives, by contrast, prioritize internal business value and have more flexible timelines. Remediation projects respond to issues (e.g. a control failure) and may have urgency but usually less external scrutiny. Regulatory projects behave differently: teams often use waterfall governance and stage gates to meet the firm deadlines. Cutting corners or missing details is dangerous; regulators expect complete traceability from each regulatory requirement to the implemented solution. Audit findings often arise when banks discover a gap between knowing the rule and effectively applying it. ### Permanent rule Treat regulatory change as mandatory, with fixed deadlines and senior oversight. Plan for full documentation and testing of compliance. Never assume you can shift a regulatory date to accommodate project delays. ### Permanent trap Treating a regulatory deadline like a usual internal deadline (i.e. deferring it or deprioritizing compliance tasks). Missing that fixed deadline invites exam findings and fines. ### Never confuse **Strategic Change** — voluntary, business-driven initiatives (may adjust scope/deadlines based on ROI). --- **Regulatory Change** — mandatory compliance projects, externally imposed with firm deadlines and audit requirements. ### No delta Across jurisdictions, the nature of regulatory projects is the same: non-negotiable effective dates and mandatory compliance. Each regulator may set different dates, but the principle of fixed deadline and required audit evidence does not change.

title: Stakeholders in Bank Change Programs
one_screen: Successful change requires early and ongoing involvement of all impacted groups: business owners (front-line and process managers), risk and compliance, finance, IT/operations, data/model owners, internal audit and (where needed) the regulator.
bodyText: A bank change program involves many stakeholders. **Business owners** (line-of-business managers, product owners) define requirements. **Risk management** teams (credit, market, operational risk) must approve changes affecting risk profile. **Finance** stakeholders (finance, accounting) need to assess cost, budget impact, and reporting changes. **Technology/IT** teams design and build the solution. **Data owners** or **model owners** must be involved when data or risk models change, to align logic and validation. **Internal Audit** should be aware early – auditors will later review that controls and procedures were properly implemented. Finally, the **Regulator** (or compliance team, if working with external regulators) often signs off on regulatory changes or reviews evidence to ensure requirements are met. A BA bridges all these groups, collecting input and keeping them aligned. For example, a new risk-reporting requirement needs review by business (for accuracy), risk (for methodology), finance (for impact on reports), IT (for system changes), and model validation (for calculations). Missing a key stakeholder can derail a project; for instance, if IT or audit are not included until late, critical requirements (like data lineage or evidence logs) might be missed. ### Permanent rule Include all relevant stakeholders early and often. Document each group’s inputs and approvals. If a group (e.g. internal audit, model validation) is required to sign off on compliance, involve them from the start to avoid rework. ### Permanent trap Assuming one person can “speak for” multiple stakeholder groups or ignoring a group’s needs. A common mistake is treating the business as the only stakeholder and failing to involve risk or audit until late in the project. ### Never confuse **Internal Audit** — the bank’s own independent check on controls and procedures (internal governance function). --- **Regulator** — the external authority enforcing compliance. Both review the project, but Internal Audit is part of the bank’s governance, whereas the Regulator is an external enforcer. ### No delta Stakeholder categories are universal in banking. All regulators expect a bank’s project to involve line management, risk/compliance, IT, finance, audit, etc. The names of groups may vary (e.g. FCA vs SEC), but the roles are similar.

title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
one_screen: Elicitation is gathering information on what stakeholders need.  Techniques include structured interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, surveys, and prototyping, chosen based on context and participant availability.
bodyText: Requirements elicitation is the process of discovering and collecting requirements from stakeholders. Common techniques: - **Interviews:** One-on-one meetings with SMEs or users to dig into specific needs. Structured interviews (with a prepared agenda and questions) are most common for detailed requirements. - **Workshops/JAD sessions:** Facilitated group sessions where stakeholders discuss processes or brainstorm solutions. Good for aligning different groups. - **Observation:** Watch users perform their real tasks (e.g. via screen-share or on-site). This uncovers implicit knowledge (like workarounds) that users might not mention. - **Document analysis:** Review existing documents, process flows, reports or contracts. This can elicit requirements without taking too much stakeholder time. - **Surveys/questionnaires:** Useful when many stakeholders are involved or geographically distributed. A survey can quickly gather input (quantitative or qualitative) from a broad group. - **Prototyping or demos:** Using mock-ups or existing systems to elicit feedback. Stakeholders react to a design, refining requirements. Each technique suits different situations. For example, if requirements are unclear and stakeholders are decentralized, a workshop may help align everyone. If SMEs are few but busy, thorough interviews with prepared questions are best. Observing users can catch missing steps in processes. The BA should mix and match techniques as needed, rather than relying on one method. ### Permanent rule Select elicitation methods that fit the situation. Always prepare thoroughly (set agendas, define questions). Use multiple techniques for cross-checking: e.g. interview a user and verify by process observation. ### Permanent trap Relying on a single method in isolation. For example, skipping document review and inundating busy stakeholders with questions they already answered in existing documentation, or doing only interviews and missing contradictory data in systems. ### Never confuse **Interview** vs **Workshop**: An *Interview* is a one-on-one or small-group discussion for in-depth detail; a *Workshop* is a facilitated group meeting to reach consensus or brainstorm. They both gather input but are different formats and scopes. ### No delta Elicitation techniques are the same globally; only local languages or frameworks vary, not the methods themselves.

title: Interviewing Time-Pressed Subject Matter Experts
one_screen: SMEs are often busy and short on time.  Always prepare an agenda and pre-reads, ask targeted questions, and build credibility so even a short meeting is productive.
bodyText: When interviewing an SME who “does not have time,” preparation is key. Before the meeting, research the topic, study any existing documentation, and send a concise agenda or questionnaire in advance. Start by explaining the project’s purpose and how their input will be used; this shows respect and gains their cooperation. In the meeting, ask clear, focused questions. Prioritize questions so the most critical ones get asked first. If possible, schedule short, focused sessions (e.g. 30 minutes) and stick to that time. Always come with an agenda and demonstrate that you’ve “done your homework” — SMEs should not hear questions that could have been answered by your own prep. Use techniques like the *5 Whys* or scenario walkthroughs to get deep insight quickly. If an SME can’t meet face-to-face, consider email questions or quick confirmations to capture their knowledge. ### Permanent rule Treat every SME meeting as valuable and limited. Go in prepared and respectful of their time. Always document answers immediately, and confirm understanding before ending. ### Permanent trap Entering an SME meeting without preparation, or hoping to get detailed answers by casually catching them off guard. Another mistake is not validating their time constraints; for example, scheduling an hour when only 15 minutes is feasible. ### Never confuse **Project Sponsor** vs **Subject Matter Expert (SME)**: A *Sponsor* is the executive or business champion who funds the project. An *SME* is a technical or functional expert providing detailed knowledge. A sponsor’s role is strategic; an SME’s is informational. They are often mixed up by new BAs. ### No delta These interpersonal techniques are universal. Bank SMEs in any country have limited time, so the approach to interviewing them is the same.

title: Process Mapping (As-Is vs To-Be)
one_screen: Process mapping diagrams the workflow of a process.  Mapping the current “as-is” process clarifies existing steps and bottlenecks; the “to-be” map lays out the improved future workflow.  Visualizing both highlights where changes are needed.
bodyText: A **process map** is a visual diagram of the steps in a business process. Common forms include flowcharts or swimlane diagrams. To create one, identify all activities, decisions, and participants. An *As-Is* map documents how things currently work; it may reveal inefficiencies, handoffs or delays. For example, an As-Is map of loan approval might show multiple manual checks. A *To-Be* map sketches the proposed future process, reflecting improvements (automation, parallel steps, elimination of waste). For instance, automating checks in the loan process would be shown as a direct flow to approval. In practice, start with an As-Is map to ensure everyone agrees on the current process. Then discuss the To-Be process: ask how tasks can be done more efficiently or with fewer steps. Document both maps and annotate issues. The difference between As-Is and To-Be shows exactly what will change. ### Permanent rule Always create an accurate As-Is process map first, then derive the To-Be. The As-Is baseline is needed to measure improvement and avoid missing steps. ### Permanent trap Jumping straight to designing the new process without fully mapping the As-Is. This often leads to overlooking current constraints or hidden steps, resulting in gaps in the solution. ### Never confuse **As-Is Process** — the current state workflow (often flawed or manual). --- **To-Be Process** — the future, improved workflow. They are frequently mixed up if one tries to innovate without understanding the current process. ### No delta Process mapping methodology is the same everywhere. Tools or notation (BPMN vs simple flowchart) may vary, but the concept of As-Is vs To-Be does not.

title: Root Cause Analysis
one_screen: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a method to find the underlying cause of a problem or error, not just its symptoms.  Techniques like “5 Whys” and fishbone diagrams are used to dig down to the true source of an issue.
bodyText: When a process fails or a requirement isn’t met, RCA helps prevent recurrence by fixing the core issue. The BA collects data about the problem, then uses a structured approach: for example, the **5 Whys** technique simply asks “Why?” repeatedly until the fundamental cause is found. Or use a **Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram**, where the team brainstorms possible causes in categories (People, Process, Systems, etc.) and traces them back to root factors. For instance, if a loan payment is missed, an RCA might reveal that data mismatches caused a calculation error (one of many possible answers). The BA should lead the team through questioning until the real cause (e.g. a misconfigured data field) is identified. Document findings in an action plan to resolve the root issue and not just the symptom. ### Permanent rule Always go deeper: fix the root cause, not just the immediate error. Use structured RCA (5 Whys, fishbone, flow analysis) to uncover underlying factors. ### Permanent trap Stopping the analysis when a temporary fix is found. For example, just patching a software bug (symptom) without discovering that it was caused by a flawed business rule mapping. ### Never confuse **Symptom** vs **Root Cause**: A *Symptom* is the visible error (e.g. a broken report). The *Root Cause* is the underlying reason (e.g. a missing data mapping rule). They are often mistakenly treated as the same. ### No delta RCA techniques apply in all industries. The concept of probing “why” multiple times or using a fishbone diagram is universal.

title: Requirements Traceability (Matrix)
one_screen: A traceability matrix links each requirement through design, code and testing.  It ensures every requirement (especially regulatory ones) is accounted for and verified.  This audit trail of requirements-to-tests is vital for regulators and audits.
bodyText: A **Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)** is usually a table or tool output mapping each requirement to its related artifacts (design specifications, code modules, test cases, test results). The BA or project manager creates/maintains the RTM. It guarantees that each requirement was implemented and tested. In banking, this is critical: regulators or auditors will want proof that every regulation-driven requirement has been satisfied. For example, if a requirement says “calculate capital ratio per Basel rules,” the RTM will show the design document section that implements it, the code module or report name, and the test cases that verify it. At audit time, the RTM provides a single view showing “Basel Cap Ratio req ➔ System Design ➔ Code ➔ Test Passed”. Traceability enforces discipline: if a requirement lacks test coverage, the matrix shows it. Banks often use the RTM to prove compliance. A comprehensive RTM helps avoid scope leakage and missed requirements. ### Permanent rule Maintain full end-to-end traceability of every requirement, especially regulatory ones. The RTM must be started early and updated continuously. Each requirement should map to at least one test case that passes. ### Permanent trap Trying to build traceability after the fact or only partially tracing requirements. For example, failing to link a regulatory requirement to a specific test, then being unable to show auditors how it was verified. ### Never confuse **Requirements Traceability Matrix** vs **Test Plan**: The *Traceability Matrix* maps requirements to tests and design. A *Test Plan* outlines the overall testing approach and schedule. They are different documents: the RTM is evidence, the test plan is strategy. ### No delta Banks in every jurisdiction must provide evidence of testing against requirements. The RTM concept is universal; differences lie only in which regulations’ requirements are in scope.

title: Business Requirements Document (BRD)
one_screen: The BRD captures *what* the business wants and *why*, including objectives, scope, stakeholders, and high-level requirements. It **must not** include solution design or technical details. Each requirement should have acceptance criteria.
bodyText: A **Business Requirements Document (BRD)** is the formal specification of business needs. It typically contains an executive summary, background, business objectives (e.g. compliance goals), scope, assumptions, and a list of requirements from the business perspective. Requirements in a BRD may include functional needs (e.g. “system shall generate monthly reports by day 5”) and non-functional needs (e.g. performance, audit trails). Importantly, the BRD states *what* is needed, not *how* to build it. It avoids technical solution detail (that belongs in a functional spec). Each requirement in the BRD should be clear and include acceptance criteria (conditions for success). For instance, instead of saying “system should be fast,” a BRD requirement would say “System must respond to user queries within 2 seconds” (with that criterion). This precision avoids ambiguity and ensures testability. Also include references to regulatory rules if applicable, and note any impacts (e.g. compliance reporting). ### Permanent rule A BRD defines *business needs and constraints*. It must not prescribe the solution. Document each requirement with its own acceptance criteria to make it verifiable. ### Permanent trap Mixing requirements with design. For example, writing “the system shall use rule X to calculate fee” (that’s a design decision) instead of “calculate fee per business rule.” Also avoid low-level detail or UI mockups in the BRD. ### Never confuse **Business Requirements** vs **Functional Specification**: A *Business Requirement* describes what the business must have (high-level need or rule). A *Functional Specification* details how the system will fulfill those needs. They are different deliverables; the BRD should not become a development spec. ### No delta What goes into a business requirements document (objectives, scope, requirements with criteria) is the same everywhere. Regulators may want documentation, but the BRD itself is a project artifact, not jurisdiction-specific.

title: Functional Specifications vs Business Requirements
one_screen: **Business requirements** state *what* is needed, while **functional specifications** describe *how* the system will meet those needs.  A business requirement is high-level (e.g. “produce regulatory report X”), whereas a functional spec details the software logic, screens, or data elements to implement it. The BRD avoids technical detail.
bodyText: Once the business requirements are agreed, the next step is often a detailed functional specification (or functional requirements document). In the functional spec, analysts or developers spell out how each business need will be met technically: database fields, algorithms, screen designs, API calls, etc. For example, a business requirement might be “notify managers of high-risk trades.” The functional spec would describe the notification module, threshold parameters, and user interface. In practice, keep these separate: the BA focuses on business needs, while solution designers write the functional spec. The BRD should remain at a business level “without excessive technical detail”. Any technical content needed for implementation goes into the functional specification. ### Permanent rule Business requirements (in the BRD) and functional specifications are distinct. The BRD should capture *what and why*. Details of *how* to meet those requirements (logic, UIs, data formats) belong in the functional spec after the BRD is approved. ### Permanent trap Allowing design to creep into the BRD or holding back needed functional detail. For instance, adding a database table definition to the BRD is mixing layers. ### Never confuse **Business Requirement** — a high-level need or rule that the solution must satisfy (e.g., “report X must include all customers over 60 days delinquent”). --- **Functional Specification** — the technical design documenting how the system will achieve that requirement (e.g., database queries, user interface fields, business logic). They get mixed up if a BA starts writing implementation detail in the BRD. ### No delta This separation of concerns is standard practice everywhere. Every bank’s BA should follow the principle regardless of jurisdiction.

title: Data Mapping Specification
one_screen: A data mapping spec is a field-by-field table linking each source field to a target field, including data type and the transformation rule.  It documents exactly how data moves or is converted from the old system to the new.
bodyText: For data migrations or integration, a **Data Mapping Specification** lists every data element to be transferred. Each row typically has: source table/field, source data type, target table/field, target data type, and *Transformation Logic/Business Rules*. For example, a mapping might say `SRC.CUST_ID (VARCHAR)` maps to `CUST.ACCOUNT_NUMBER (String)` with rule “pad with leading zeros to length 15”. Or “DOB (YYYYMMDD) → Birthdate (YYYY-MM-DD)” to reformat dates. This document serves as the *golden source* for developers and testers to implement and verify data flow. In banking, precise mapping is critical (e.g. for customer data, transactions). Missing a transformation can lead to errors or compliance issues. ### Permanent rule Document every data element and its transformation explicitly. Include data types and any business rule (e.g. code-to-description mapping) for each field. ### Permanent trap Assuming simple copy (source to target) for all fields. Some fields require non-trivial transformation (format changes, code mappings) which must be written down, or testers cannot verify correctness. ### Never confuse **Source Field** vs **Target Field** in mapping: A *Source Field* is the field in the existing (origin) system. A *Target Field* is where it goes in the new system. Keep straight which is which when writing the spec. ### No delta Data mapping documentation is the same process in any country or system. The need for clear source-to-target definitions is universal.

title: Non-Functional Requirements (Performance, Retention, Auditability)
one_screen: Non-functional requirements define *how* the system performs: its quality attributes like speed, security, data retention, and audit capabilities. In banking, **auditability** (e.g. full logging and data retention) is often mandated for compliance.
bodyText: Non-functional requirements (NFRs) cover attributes not captured by functional specs. Key NFRs in banking projects include: - **Performance:** e.g. “System must handle 1000 concurrent users with response <2s.” - **Security & Compliance:** data encryption, access controls, KYC/AML checks, GDPR or similar data privacy. - **Availability:** e.g. “99.9% uptime required.” - **Data Retention:** how long data (or logs) must be kept (often 5–7 years or more). - **Auditability:** ability to trace actions – full logging of transactions and changes. Regulators explicitly require audit trails on changes. For example, a BA noted for a bank onboarding project that auditability (full action logs retained 7+ years) was a key NFR. Non-functional requirements are critical: even if the functionality is correct, failure in security or audit logging can invalidate a project. In regulated change, treat NFRs like compliance: put them in the requirement list and test for them. ### Permanent rule Always capture NFRs explicitly (security, performance, reliability, legal/policy requirements). In banking, *auditability* (e.g. detailed logs and retention policies) is first-class: include it as a requirement early. ### Permanent trap Assuming NFRs will be “obvious” or handled later. A common error is neglecting to require sufficient audit logging or forgetting to enforce retention, only to fail compliance checks later. ### Never confuse **Functional Requirement** vs **Non-Functional Requirement**: A *Functional Requirement* describes what the system does (specific features). A *Non-Functional Requirement* describes constraints or qualities (like speed, security). For example, “generate monthly report” is functional; “report generation shall complete within 5 minutes” is non-functional. ### No delta The categories of performance, security, retention and audit requirements are the same across banks worldwide. Regulatory laws differ (e.g. GDPR vs CCPA), but the concept of NFRs is universal.

title: Testable Acceptance Criteria
one_screen: Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions that define when a requirement is met.  Well-crafted criteria are clear, concise, and objectively verifiable.
bodyText: Each requirement (or user story) needs acceptance criteria that describe exactly what “done” means. They are written from the user’s perspective: e.g. “The search function returns results that match 100% or partially matching the query” (as in one example). According to Atlassian, acceptance criteria are “clear, concise, and testable statements” that define what success looks like. They should be measurable: instead of vague terms (“fast”, “user-friendly”), use objective thresholds (e.g. “90% of transactions processed within 2 seconds”). Each criterion should map to one or more executable tests. Good acceptance criteria eliminate ambiguity. They align development and QA teams and allow stakeholders to verify requirements. As one guide puts it, they define *“what success looks like”* and “translate the purpose into explicit, verifiable requirements”. For regulators, acceptance criteria often double as test cases to demonstrate compliance. ### Permanent rule Write acceptance criteria that are specific and measurable. Each criterion must be objectively verifiable (e.g. through a test or demo). If you can’t define a pass/fail condition, refine the requirement. ### Permanent trap Vague criteria. For example, “The system must be user-friendly” or “Reports should load quickly” are not testable. Also avoid combining multiple conditions into one criterion. Each criterion should stand alone (independent). ### Never confuse **Acceptance Criteria** vs **Test Case**: *Acceptance Criteria* are the high-level conditions to meet for a requirement to be accepted. A *Test Case* is a detailed script with steps to verify those criteria. They serve related purposes (criteria shape tests) but are not the same thing. ### No delta The practice of defining testable acceptance criteria is universal across methodologies and jurisdictions.

title: User Stories and Acceptance in a Regulated Context
one_screen: In agile development, user stories (“As a user, I want…”) drive increments.  In a regulated project, each story’s acceptance criteria must tie back to formal requirements and evidence.  You may still use stories, but supplement them with thorough documentation and approvals for audit purposes.
bodyText: User stories are a popular agile format to describe functionality. However, in regulated banking change, “just” having user stories is not enough for audit evidence. For example, a story like “As an accountant I want to generate report X” must be backed by a formal requirement in the BRD or similar doc for traceability. The acceptance criteria for each story should explicitly cover any regulatory rule or business rule involved. In practice, BAs in banks often write user stories for the development team, but also maintain a requirements traceability matrix linking each story to the original business requirement or regulation. All acceptance criteria must be documented and tested; regulators may request proof that each story’s scope was approved by risk/compliance. If agile ceremonies (like demos) are used, capture their sign-off too. In short, use user stories for agile development, but never skip the required artifacts (requirements docs, trace matrix, approvals) needed in the regulated context. ### Permanent rule When using agile user stories in a regulated project, ensure each story and criterion has formal backing. Treat each as “level 1” requirements in the traceability matrix, and secure formal approval on them. ### Permanent trap Assuming “agile = no documentation.” In regulated change, you cannot omit documentation. Don’t rely solely on Jira tickets or casual “demo approval”; record story acceptance formally. ### Never confuse **User Story** vs **Regulatory Requirement**: A *User Story* is a short description of a feature from an end-user’s perspective (agile format). A *Regulatory Requirement* is an explicit compliance mandate that must be met. User stories may implement a regulatory requirement, but the regulator cares about proof of the requirement being met, not just the story text. ### No delta This principle applies everywhere. Whether in India, US, or EU, using agile in regulation-heavy projects requires additional documentation.

title: Testing Lifecycle (Unit, System, Integration, UAT)
one_screen: A typical banking IT change goes through multiple test phases: Unit testing (by developers), Integration/System testing (by QA/IT), and User Acceptance Testing (by business).  Each phase has different owners and objectives.
bodyText: The testing process is layered: - **Unit Testing:** done by developers on individual code modules. Ensures each component works as intended. - **Integration Testing:** QA or IT tests combined modules or subsystems. Checks interfaces between components. - **System Testing:** QA tests the complete system against requirements (functional and non-functional). - **User Acceptance Testing (UAT):** Business users test end-to-end business scenarios in a production-like environment. UAT is led by the business (operations, product, compliance teams). UAT ensures the system meets real business needs before go-live. Each test type requires different participants: developers own unit tests, QA owns system/integration tests, and business stakeholders perform UAT. Testing each phase is critical: skipping system test and jumping to UAT, for instance, risks missing defects that developers should have caught. ### Permanent rule Follow all test phases in order and involve the right people. Use unit and system tests to catch defects early, and let end users validate the solution in UAT. ### Permanent trap Treating UAT as the first time the business sees the solution. If unit/integration tests are inadequate, UAT will be overwhelmed with obvious issues. ### Never confuse **System Test** vs **User Acceptance Test (UAT)**: *System Test* is executed by QA/IT to verify the software meets the specified requirements. *UAT* is done by business users to verify the system meets their needs in real-world scenarios. ### No delta These test phases and roles are standard in all banking projects globally.

title: Test Planning and Test Packs
one_screen: A test plan defines the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of testing. Test packs (test cases and data) list the specific scenarios with expected outcomes.  For each requirement, predefined test cases and datasets must be prepared before testing begins.
bodyText: Before execution, the BA (often with QA) creates a **Test Plan**: it includes test objectives, types of testing, environment details, schedule, and responsibilities. The plan ensures everyone knows what will be tested and when. Key to this is preparing **test packs**: collections of test cases and test data with expected results. For example, a pack for a regulatory report change might include sample transactions (input data) and the exact numbers expected in the output. In regulated projects, predefined test data is especially important: you must demonstrate that for each scenario, you know the “right answer” in advance. This way, testers (or auditors reviewing UAT) can verify correctness efficiently. The BA’s role is to help identify all required scenarios and define the expected results (often consulting SMEs or model owners for calculations). Testers then use this pack during UAT to systematically execute tests. ### Permanent rule Develop detailed test cases and data (test packs) for all requirements. Each test should have the input data and the precise expected result documented. ### Permanent trap Assuming testers will figure out expected outcomes on the fly. Without a predefined expected result, testers cannot conclusively pass/fail a case, and auditors will challenge the validity of the test. ### Never confuse **Test Plan** vs **Test Case/Test Pack**: A *Test Plan* is the high-level strategy and timeline for testing. A *Test Case* (in a pack) is a specific scenario with steps and expected result. The plan is “what/when”, test cases are “how/results”. ### No delta The discipline of planning tests and defining expected results is a best practice everywhere.

title: UAT Coverage and Defect Management
one_screen: Ensure UAT covers all critical business and regulatory scenarios. Use metrics (e.g. scenario coverage %) to argue sufficiency.  Manage defects by classifying each by *severity* (technical impact) and *priority* (business urgency).
bodyText: **UAT Coverage:** The BA must confirm that UAT scenarios collectively cover all key requirements and risk areas. Typically, this is demonstrated by linking each requirement (and sub-case) to one or more UAT scenarios. In practice, teams track *scenario coverage percentage*. For example, Yethi’s core banking UAT practice uses end-to-end business scenarios (account opening, loan origination, payments) to ensure coverage. They measure how many of those planned scenarios have been executed successfully. To argue coverage is sufficient, present traceability: “Requirement X is covered by test cases TC1, TC2.” Focus on risk: prioritize testing of critical flows first. **Defect Management:** Each defect discovered in testing is logged with details. Importantly, classify it by **Severity** (the technical impact: *Critical* = system-blocker, *Major*, etc.) and **Priority** (how urgent the fix is to the business: high=must-fix, low=can wait). For example, a calculation error in a capital ratio (high severity) might also be high priority. Lowering defect list by severity/priority and reaching “0 critical open” is usually a go-live criterion. Track defects transparently: who fixes them, retest after fixes, and ensure no showstoppers remain before sign-off. ### Permanent rule Build UAT scenarios that cover *every* business requirement, especially regulatory ones. Use traceability and coverage metrics to justify adequacy. Classify and fix defects based on agreed severity/priority rules. ### Permanent trap Overconfidence that “we tested enough” without proof. Always use coverage measures or sign-offs on critical scenarios. Also, don’t mix up severity and priority – a minor typo may be low severity but could be high priority if it affects reporting. ### Never confuse **Severity** vs **Priority**: *Severity* gauges the impact of a defect on system functionality. *Priority* indicates how quickly the defect should be fixed (a business decision). They are separate measures, not synonyms. ### No delta The need for clear UAT coverage and defect triage is the same in all banks. Regulatory or not, rigorous UAT and defect classification prevent missed issues.

title: Parallel Running & Go-Live Planning
one_screen: *Parallel running* means operating the old and new systems side-by-side for a period to compare outputs. *Go-live planning* (cutover) details how to switch to the new system, including rollback steps if needed.  Both are critical in regulated transitions.
bodyText: Before decommissioning legacy processes, banks often run *both* systems in parallel to ensure the new one works correctly. For example, a bank might process a day’s transactions in both the old system and the new IFRS-compliant system and compare the results. This parallel run period (sometimes months) builds confidence and provides audit evidence that the new outputs are accurate. It also allows real data to exercise the system without immediate risk. The *go-live plan* (cutover plan) is executed once parallel runs are complete. It is a detailed schedule: which data migration steps to perform, which systems to shut down/start up, and who is responsible for each action. The plan must include *rollback procedures*: if a critical issue occurs, how to revert to the old system to prevent business impact. For example, ensure backups and change logs are ready. Roles (executive sponsor, IT lead, BA, etc.) must be assigned for go/no-go decisions and communication to stakeholders. ### Permanent rule Include parallel running and dual-reporting as part of implementation. Plan go-live steps meticulously and always have a tested rollback strategy. Confirm decision criteria (e.g. “all parallel outputs match 99%”) before full cutover. ### Permanent trap Assuming go-live will succeed without rehearsal. A frequent mistake is not planning for failures – e.g. no rollback or contingency plan. Also failing to run both systems long enough to catch issues. ### Never confuse **Parallel Run** vs **Dual Reporting**: A *Parallel Run* is running old and new systems at the same time to validate output. *Dual Reporting* is submitting reports in both old and new regimes (e.g. old accounting vs new) to regulators. They both involve duplication but serve different verification purposes. ### No delta These deployment practices are standard in banking globally, especially for compliance transitions.

title: Post-Implementation Review and Benefits Realisation
one_screen: After go-live, conduct a formal review comparing actual outcomes to planned objectives. Capture lessons learned and track whether expected benefits (cost savings, efficiency gains, compliance) are realized.
bodyText: Once the system is live and stable, a **Post-Implementation Review (PIR)** evaluates success. The BA should gather the project team and business stakeholders to review metrics and outcomes. Did the system meet the business objectives outlined in the BRD? For example, if the goal was a 50% reduction in report prep time, measure the actual improvement. Regulatory objectives (e.g. no compliance violations) must also be confirmed. Part of the PIR is **Benefits Realisation**: compare the business case predictions (e.g. lower costs, better risk metrics) to reality. If benefits fall short, identify why. Lessons from the review should feed back into process improvements for future changes. A formal PIR also provides closure: documenting success and issues demonstrates to auditors and leadership that the project delivered as intended (or what corrective actions are taken). ### Permanent rule Always schedule a post-launch review. It should include all key stakeholders, revisit requirements and scope, and check actual performance and risk metrics against targets. ### Permanent trap Skipping the review or only doing technical validation. Don’t forget to measure business impact. For example, installing a new compliance module but never checking if compliance reporting is actually more accurate counts as incomplete implementation. ### Never confuse **Post-Implementation Review** vs **Project Closure**: A *PIR* examines project outcomes and lessons. *Project Closure* is the administrative final step (sign-offs, documentation archive). Both are needed, but PIR focuses on evaluation and benefits tracking. ### No delta Reviewing outcomes and realising benefits is a recommended practice worldwide, not specific to one jurisdiction.

title: Waterfall vs Agile in Banking
one_screen: Waterfall (stage-gate) and Agile (iterative) are both used in banks.  Regulatory changes often lean waterfall: fixed scope and deadlines drive sequential phases (requirements→design→build→test). Agile is better for evolving requirements, but must be adapted for compliance needs.
bodyText: Many banks use waterfall for compliance projects because regulators expect detailed plans and sign-offs. As one analyst notes, banks “generally set up regulatory projects in a sequential manner—finalize requirements, then design, then build, then test”. This ensures all regulatory criteria are identified and reviewed upfront. However, waterfall can struggle if requirements change mid-project (which happens frequently). Agile frameworks allow incremental development and frequent feedback, which can help manage changes. In reality, banks often use hybrids: they may scope and plan a regulatory change in detail (waterfall style) but develop components iteratively, or run multiple agile sprints for low-risk modules. If using Agile, the BA still needs to document and get approval for requirements. Sprints will produce user stories, but the overall scope cannot drift beyond what’s compliant. Regulators may allow iterative delivery internally, but they expect evidence that all parts of the regulation were handled. For a fixed regulatory date, waterfall gating provides clear go/no-go points (though it risks corner-cutting under pressure). Agile’s visibility (working demos) can reassure stakeholders, but BAs must reconcile it with the formal change control needed. ### Permanent rule Choose methodology based on project nature. Regulatory changes usually require upfront planning and documentation, so use waterfall or a controlled hybrid. If adopting Agile elements, ensure deliverables and approvals still meet compliance scrutiny. ### Permanent trap Attempting a pure agile approach for a fixed-scope regulatory program without adapting (e.g. without documentation or formal sign-off). Conversely, ignoring agile techniques entirely can lead to last-minute rework. ### Never confuse **Waterfall** vs **Agile**: *Waterfall* is sequential, with completed phases (requirements→design→build→test). *Agile* is iterative and incremental, allowing requirements to evolve. They both aim to deliver systems, but differ in process: Agile values working software over docs, whereas Waterfall emphasizes planning and documentation. In banking, the line blurs, but they remain distinct approaches. ### No delta The trade-offs of waterfall vs agile are the same worldwide. Choice depends on project uncertainty and constraints, not jurisdiction. However, strict regulators may influence banks to favour waterfall-like controls.

title: Prioritisation & Estimation in Banking Projects
one_screen: Prioritize work using clear criteria (business value, risk, regulatory urgency) and defend choices with data.  Estimate tasks realistically using ranges or past data, accounting for optimism bias.
bodyText: BAs often help decide what to do first in a change program. Common prioritisation methods include *weighted scoring* (scoring features by value, cost, risk), *MoSCoW* (Must/Should/Could/Won’t), or simple *risk-first* (fix highest compliance risk first). For regulatory projects, items explicitly tied to required dates are usually top priority. Always document how you prioritized: for example, “Requirement A scored 9/10 on impact because it directly addresses a mandatory regulation” provides rationale. This transparency makes prioritisation defensible to management and auditors. For estimation, acknowledge that BAs and teams are naturally optimistic (the “planning fallacy”). Use historical data or three-point estimates (best/likely/worst) to capture uncertainty. Include a buffer for testing and integration complexities. For instance, if developing a new report took 10 days in a past project, plan 15 days for similar complexity. Clear estimation methods (e.g. story points, function points, or t-shirt sizes) help set realistic schedules and avoid last-minute scope cuts. ### Permanent rule Use objective criteria (value to business, compliance risk, regulatory deadline) in a documented prioritisation model. When estimating, always allow contingencies – it’s normal to be optimistic, so plan for known unknowns. ### Permanent trap Letting “priority” be decided by the loudest stakeholder or an incorrect assumption that all items are equally urgent. Also, giving point estimates (e.g. “5 days”) without ranges ignores uncertainty; this often leads to schedule overrun. ### Never confuse **Urgency** vs **Importance**: An *Urgent* task has a tight deadline (often regulatory or external). An *Important* task has high business value or impact. They can differ (e.g. a bug might be urgent but low importance). Prioritisation should consider both, not mistake one for the other. ### No delta Banks use the same prioritisation logic everywhere. CFOs and regulators expect clear rationale for why one feature was delayed and another accelerated.

title: Managing Scope Change with Fixed Deadlines
one_screen: In projects with immovable regulatory deadlines, handle scope changes through a formal change control process.  Assess each new requirement’s impact on timeline and scope. If the deadline cannot move, negotiate resources or de-scope non-critical items rather than slipping the date.
bodyText: Scope changes are inevitable, but on a regulatory program the deadline is set by law. Every requested change must go through a structured change request process. The BA must document the change, analyze its impact on schedule and cost, and present to the Change Control Board. If adding new requirements, either find efficiency elsewhere or request additional resources (often hard to get). The key is *trade-offs*: for example, if a late rule change is issued, you might push some non-essential enhancements to the next phase. All approved changes and their rationales should be logged in a change control log. No unapproved scope creep should occur: formal approval (by business, risk, audit) is required for anything beyond original scope. In practice, regulators expect that the project was baselined and any changes are traceable. A formal change control ensures auditors see an audit trail of decisions (who approved a change and why). ### Permanent rule Always process scope changes formally. Do not slip regulatory deadlines. If new items arise late, escalate them to executives and re-prioritize or delay less-critical work. ### Permanent trap Allowing uncontrolled additions to scope (scope creep) because of “just this one change.” Each change must consider the fixed deadline. Avoid informal side agreements to implement extra features without updating the project plan. ### Never confuse **Scope Change** vs **Scope Creep**: *Scope Change* is a formally approved modification with documented impact analysis. *Scope Creep* is uncontrolled expansion of scope. A regulated project should only have intentional scope changes through proper channels. ### No delta Change control discipline is standard in every banking regulation project. What varies by jurisdiction is the regulatory author, not how change is managed.

title: Why Regulatory Capital Exists
one_screen: Expected loss is the centre of a loss distribution; unexpected loss is the adverse loss beyond that centre. IMP-01 → a loss allowance reduces an asset's carrying amount, while capital is loss-absorbing resource against unexpected loss. Regulatory capital exists to preserve solvency when realised losses outrun earnings and recognised loss allowances.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | Prudential job | | :--- | :--- | | Expected loss | Anticipated cost of taking risk | | Allowance | Recognised reduction in an asset's carrying amount | | Earnings | First recurring source for absorbing costs and rebuilding capital | | Regulatory capital | Loss-bearing resource protecting solvency against adverse outcomes | Basel's IRB architecture makes the split visible: its risk-weight functions are calibrated to unexpected loss, while regulatory expected loss is compared separately with eligible provisions. The split is conceptual, not a claim that accounting allowance must equal regulatory expected loss. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Capital is a solvency resource against loss. It is not a substitute for recognising expected credit losses promptly. ### Never confuse [Allowance] and [Capital] **Allowance** — a measured reduction in the carrying amount of an asset for recognised credit loss. --- **Capital** — qualifying loss-absorbing resource available to bear losses and preserve solvency. ### Permanent trap Calling an allowance "capital set aside for bad loans" collapses two different objects. The allowance changes the asset and earnings; capital is the residual loss-bearing claim after those accounting effects. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The loss-distribution logic is common; accounting and prudential implementation determine how the two objects interact.

title: Loss Absorption: Going Concern to Resolution
one_screen: FND-04 → capital is not liquidity: capital absorbs losses; liquidity meets payments when due. Within capital itself, timing matters: going-concern resources absorb loss while the bank remains viable, while gone-concern resources support creditor protection and resolution after viability is lost.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Basel classifies CET1 and AT1 within Tier 1, its going-concern layer. Tier 2 is the lower-quality layer intended principally for loss absorption at non-viability or resolution. The legal trigger and write-down or conversion mechanism depend on the applicable instrument terms and resolution law. A solvent bank can still be illiquid, and an illiquid bank can temporarily remain solvent. Therefore a strong CET1 ratio does not mean the bank holds enough cash to meet tomorrow's withdrawals. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Regulatory quality depends on whether loss absorption is reliably available when required, not on whether an instrument is called equity or subordinated debt. ### Never confuse [Going-concern capital] and [Gone-concern capital] **Going-concern capital** — absorbs loss while the institution remains viable and operating. --- **Gone-concern capital** — absorbs loss principally after non-viability, failure or resolution action. ### Permanent trap Treating Tier 2 as equivalent to CET1 because both count in Total Capital ignores the timing and quality of their loss absorption. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel hierarchy. Resolution statutes and contractual non-viability mechanisms differ by jurisdiction.

title: The Capital Quality Hierarchy
one_screen: Regulatory capital is nested by quality. CET1 is the highest-quality layer; CET1 plus AT1 is Tier 1; Tier 1 plus Tier 2 is Total Capital. Because the categories are nested, lower-quality capital cannot repair a shortfall in a higher-quality requirement.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | What it contributes | Can satisfy | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | CET1 | Highest-quality, permanent going-concern loss absorption | CET1, Tier 1 and Total Capital requirements | | AT1 | Additional going-concern capacity meeting stricter permanence and loss-absorption rules than ordinary debt | Tier 1 and Total Capital, not CET1 | | Tier 2 | Lower-quality subordinated gone-concern capacity | Total Capital only | Basel global minimum ratios are themselves nested: 4.5% CET1, 6% Tier 1 and 8% Total Capital, before buffers and any jurisdictional or firm-specific additions. A bank therefore does not add 4.5 + 6 + 8 and hold 18.5% merely because three ratios are reported. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Capital quality nests upward: CET1 can meet a broader requirement, but Tier 2 cannot meet a CET1 or Tier 1 shortfall. ### Never confuse [Tier 1] and [Total Capital] **Tier 1** — CET1 plus eligible AT1. --- **Total Capital** — Tier 1 plus eligible Tier 2. ### Permanent trap Adding the CET1, Tier 1 and Total Capital minimum percentages as separate capital layers triple-counts the same higher-quality capital. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the hierarchy. Jurisdictions may set higher ratios or additional layers above the Basel minima.

title: Common Equity Tier 1
one_screen: CET1 is the highest-quality regulatory capital because it bears losses continuously and is not protected by a contractual promise of repayment. FND-03 → retained earnings accumulate profit after distributions; losses run through earnings and therefore reduce CET1 unless another qualifying capital action offsets them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism CET1 begins with qualifying common equity instruments, associated share premium, retained earnings and other eligible disclosed reserves, then applies prudential criteria and adjustments. | CET1 property | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | | Perpetual | No maturity that forces repayment | | Most subordinated claim | Losses reach common equity before senior creditors | | Distributions discretionary | Bank is not forced to pay a coupon or dividend | | Fully available for loss absorption | Capital can fall as losses are recognised | | Clear issue and repayment rules | Prevents capital disappearing through redemption | A common share can fail regulatory eligibility if its terms weaken permanence or loss absorption. Conversely, an accounting equity line is not automatically CET1 merely because it sits within shareholders' equity. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule CET1 is defined by prudential eligibility and loss-absorption characteristics, not by the accounting label "equity". ### Never confuse [Common equity] and [CET1] **Common equity** — an accounting or corporate-law description of ownership interests. --- **CET1** — the subset of highest-quality capital recognised after Basel eligibility criteria and regulatory adjustments. ### Permanent trap Using total shareholders' equity as the CET1 numerator without checking eligibility, filters and deductions can overstate prudential capital. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the core Basel characteristics. National company law and local transposition determine the exact legal instruments that can meet those characteristics.

title: Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2
one_screen: AT1 and Tier 2 extend loss-bearing capacity beyond common equity, but they do so with lower regulatory quality. AT1 remains within going-concern Tier 1; Tier 2 is principally the gone-concern layer. Neither category exists merely because a security is marketed as a hybrid or subordinated bond.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Feature | AT1 | Tier 2 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Place in stack | Tier 1 | Total Capital below Tier 1 | | Maturity | Perpetual under Basel eligibility | Minimum original maturity requirements; recognition amortises near maturity | | Distributions | Fully discretionary, non-cumulative where required | Contractual servicing can exist subject to eligibility | | Subordination | Deeply subordinated | Subordinated to depositors and general creditors | | Loss absorption | Going-concern mechanisms plus non-viability requirements | Principally non-viability / gone-concern | | Redemption | Subject to regulatory conditions and no expectation of repayment | Subject to eligibility and supervisory conditions | Basel requires detailed instrument terms because a security that looks equity-like economically may still contain redemption incentives, step-ups, payment obligations or other features inconsistent with regulatory capital. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule An instrument counts only if its legal terms satisfy the applicable regulatory-capital criteria throughout the period for which recognition is claimed. ### Never confuse [AT1] and [Tier 2] **AT1** — additional going-concern Tier 1 capital that does not qualify as CET1. --- **Tier 2** — lower-ranking capital recognised toward Total Capital and designed principally for gone-concern loss absorption. ### Permanent trap Assuming every perpetual bond is AT1 or every subordinated bond is Tier 2 ignores the eligibility tests that make the instrument genuinely loss absorbing. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel categories. Instrument documentation, tax treatment, resolution powers and national eligibility rules create implementation differences.

title: From Accounting Equity to Regulatory Capital
one_screen: Accounting equity answers a reporting question; regulatory CET1 answers whether an amount is sufficiently reliable and available to absorb prudential loss. Regulatory adjustments therefore remove, filter or limit items that could disappear in stress, create double counting or produce capital that is not economically available to the banking group.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Common Basel adjustments include goodwill and specified intangible assets, certain deferred tax assets, own-credit effects, defined-benefit pension items and investments in the capital of financial institutions. Threshold treatments apply to specified items rather than making every such balance an automatic full deduction. The common principle is availability. If an asset's value depends on the bank remaining profitable, or if the same capital is counted by two regulated entities, gross accounting equity can overstate the resources genuinely available in stress. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A capital ratio uses qualifying regulatory capital after adjustments, not gross book equity. ### Never confuse [Book equity] and [Regulatory CET1] **Book equity** — equity measured under the applicable accounting framework. --- **Regulatory CET1** — highest-quality eligible capital after prudential filters, deductions and threshold treatments. ### Permanent trap Treating goodwill as loss-absorbing capital because it increases accounting assets ignores that its stressed realisable value may vanish exactly when capital is needed. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the principle. Detailed deductions, thresholds and transitional treatments are jurisdiction-specific implementation choices.

title: Where Allowances Meet Capital
one_screen: IMP-01 owns the object distinction: allowance is a reduction in an asset's carrying amount; capital is loss-absorbing resource. This atom owns the transmission between them. A higher credit-loss allowance reduces earnings or opening retained earnings, which usually reduces CET1; prudential rules can then make further capital adjustments without turning the allowance itself into capital.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The same economic deterioration can also raise RWA through rating migration, default treatment or changed exposure characteristics. Capital ratios can therefore weaken through both numerator and denominator. The prudential framework then asks a separate question: how much of the accounting provision is eligible for a specific regulatory-capital treatment? Under IRB, that question becomes the expected-loss-versus-eligible-provision comparison owned by CAP-08. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The allowance affects capital mainly by changing earnings or equity; any regulatory recognition of provisions is a second prudential step. ### Never confuse [Allowance effect on CET1] and [Allowance counted as capital] **Allowance effect on CET1** — accounting loss recognition reduces retained earnings and therefore the CET1 base. --- **Allowance counted as capital** — a separate and limited prudential treatment that exists only where the capital rules permit it. ### Permanent trap Saying "provisions increase capital because they absorb losses" misses the first-order accounting effect: creating the provision generally reduces profit and CET1. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the balance-sheet transmission. The regulatory treatment of provision shortfalls, excess provisions and transitional relief differs by approach and jurisdiction.

title: Regulatory Expected Loss and Eligible Provisions
one_screen: CR-09 → expected loss is a governed PD/LGD/EAD quantity; IMP-01 → an accounting allowance is not capital. Under IRB, Basel nevertheless compares regulatory expected loss with eligible provisions so expected credit loss is not silently left uncovered or double-counted in the capital stack.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Basel CRE35 defines total eligible provisions for IRB exposures and requires the comparison with total regulatory EL. CAP30 requires the full shortfall, where regulatory EL exceeds eligible provisions, to be deducted from CET1. Where provisions exceed EL, the excess may receive limited Tier 2 recognition subject to the framework. This is not an accounting true-up. Regulatory EL and accounting ECL can differ in horizon, parameter calibration, default treatment and objective. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A provision shortfall reduces CET1 because the prudential EL amount is not fully covered by eligible provisions. ### Never confuse [Regulatory expected loss] and [Accounting ECL] **Regulatory expected loss** — prudential quantity defined inside the IRB capital framework. --- **Accounting ECL** — loss allowance measured under the applicable accounting or prudential provisioning architecture. ### Permanent trap Comparing lifetime accounting ECL directly with one-year IRB EL as though the two should reconcile mechanically ignores different definitions and objectives. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel IRB mechanism. It is relevant only where the jurisdiction permits IRB for the exposure concerned.

title: ECL Transition and Regulatory Capital Relief
one_screen: A new ECL regime can create an immediate opening-equity hit before the underlying loans have changed overnight. Transitional capital relief smooths that prudential shock; it does not undo the allowance. **As at August 2026**, RBI's final ECL Directions are issued but not yet in force: they commence on **1 April 2027** and permit a declining CET1 add-back through **31 March 2031**.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism RBI transition: | Financial year | Maximum fraction of transitional adjustment added back to CET1 | | :--- | ---: | | 2027-28 | 4/5 | | 2028-29 | 3/5 | | 2029-30 | 2/5 | | 2030-31 | 1/5 | | 2031-32 onward | Nil | The add-back is net of applicable taxes. RBI states that the recognised amount flows through, as appropriate, to Tier 1 and Total Capital and therefore derived measures, but it is not Tier 2, cannot reduce standardised-approach exposure amounts and cannot reduce the leverage exposure measure. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Transition relief changes regulatory capital recognition; it does not reverse, defer or reduce the ECL allowance required by the provisioning framework. ### Never confuse [ECL transition adjustment] and [CET1 add-back] **ECL transition adjustment** — the opening-equity effect arising from the change in provisioning basis. --- **CET1 add-back** — temporary prudential recognition of a declining fraction of that effect. ### Permanent trap Reporting only the transitional CET1 ratio hides the fully-loaded economics. RBI therefore requires disclosure of the capital and leverage impact relative to the no-transition position. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) **As at August 2026:** final rule issued 27 April 2026; effective 1 April 2027. Future phase-out steps run through 31 March 2031. This is a rule with a future commencement date, not a proposal.

title: Capital Ratio Anatomy
one_screen: A capital ratio combines two governed quantities: qualifying capital in the numerator and risk-weighted assets in the denominator. A bank can lose capital adequacy because the numerator falls, because RWA rises, or because both move against it at the same time.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Change | Ratio effect, all else equal | | :--- | :--- | | CET1 decreases | CET1 ratio decreases | | RWA increases | All RWA-based ratios decrease | | New eligible capital issued | Relevant numerator increases | | Exposure runoff / lower risk weight | RWA may decrease | | Provision expense | CET1 may decrease through retained earnings | | Credit migration | RWA may increase | The Basel minima are expressed as ratios to RWA: 4.5% CET1, 6% Tier 1 and 8% Total Capital before buffers and local additions. Buffers do not change the denominator; they raise the amount of CET1 the bank must maintain above the minimum stack. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule A capital ratio cannot be interpreted from the numerator alone; RWA is part of the prudential measurement. ### Never confuse [Capital amount] and [Capital ratio] **Capital amount** — currency value of qualifying regulatory capital. --- **Capital ratio** — qualifying regulatory capital divided by the prescribed RWA denominator. ### Permanent trap Explaining a falling CET1 ratio only by "losses reduced CET1" can miss denominator inflation from credit migration, market moves or model changes. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the ratio mechanics. Binding minima, buffers and RWA methodologies vary by jurisdiction.

title: Risk Weights and Risk-Weighted Assets
one_screen: FND-11 → exposure is the amount at risk under a defined measurement basis. A risk weight scales that exposure into regulatory RWA; it is not a forecast of the percentage that will default or be lost.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Quantity | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | Exposure amount | Regulatory amount to which the capital treatment applies | | Risk weight | Prudential scaling factor | | RWA | Exposure translated into the risk-based denominator | | RWA density | RWA divided by a chosen exposure measure | A 100% risk weight means one unit of exposure creates one unit of RWA before other adjustments. It does not mean 100% PD, 100% LGD or 100% expected loss. Likewise, a low risk weight can reduce risk-based capital without reducing the leverage exposure. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Risk weights calibrate prudential capital intensity; they do not estimate expected credit loss. ### Never confuse [Risk weight] and [Probability of default] **Risk weight** — regulatory scaling factor used in calculating RWA. --- **Probability of default** — likelihood of default over a governed horizon. ### Permanent trap Reading a 150% risk weight as "the regulator expects a 150% loss" confuses a capital calibration with a loss forecast. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the arithmetic. Exposure classes, prescribed weights and permitted methodologies differ by rulebook.

title: The RWA Engines
one_screen: Total RWA is not produced by one universal risk-weight formula. Separate prudential engines measure credit, market, operational and CVA-related risks under their own rules, then feed a common risk-based capital denominator.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Engine | Risk captured | Typical object | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Credit risk | Obligor, issuer or counterparty failure to perform | Banking-book loans, securities, counterparty exposures | | Market risk | Adverse moves in market risk factors | Trading-book positions | | Operational risk | Failed processes, people, systems or external events | Bank-wide operational activity | | CVA risk | Change in credit valuation adjustment | Covered derivative counterparty positions | CVA risk is not merely default risk under another name. Counterparty default capital addresses failure to perform; CVA capital addresses valuation changes caused by counterparty credit spread and related risk before or without default. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Each risk engine must be measured under its own prudential methodology before aggregation. ### Never confuse [Counterparty default risk] and [CVA risk] **Counterparty default risk** — loss because the counterparty fails to perform. --- **CVA risk** — loss from changes in the market value of the credit valuation adjustment. ### Permanent trap Applying a loan-style risk weight to operational or market risk ignores that those risk types have separate capital methodologies. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the architecture. Implementation dates and detailed approaches can differ; those differences belong to local rulebooks.

title: Standardised Credit Risk: Exposure to RWA
one_screen: CR-01/02 → obligor and facility are different risk objects. Under the standardised approach, the prudential rulebook classifies the exposure, determines the regulatory exposure amount and applies prescribed risk drivers and weights rather than allowing the bank's own PD/LGD model to generate the core capital requirement.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Standardised does not mean one weight for every exposure. Sovereigns, banks, corporates, retail, real estate, defaulted exposures and specialised lending can follow different rulebook treatments. External ratings are only one possible input and are used only where the applicable framework permits them. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule The regulator standardises the methodology; the resulting RWA can still be highly risk-sensitive across exposure classes. ### Never confuse [Standardised approach] and [External rating] **Standardised approach** — supervisor-prescribed capital methodology. --- **External rating** — one permitted input for specified exposures under specified conditions. ### Permanent trap Assigning one default weight to every unrated corporate exposure ignores exposure-class rules, due diligence and jurisdictional implementation. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) **As at August 2026:** RBI's final revised Standardised Approach was issued 27 April 2026 and comes into force **1 April 2027**. It is a final rule with future commencement, not a proposal. #### UK (PRA) **As at August 2026:** final Basel 3.1 rules are issued and commence **1 January 2027**. #### EU **As at August 2026:** CRR3 standardised credit-risk reforms have applied since **1 January 2025**. #### US **As at August 2026:** revisions issued on 19 March 2026 are proposals, not implemented rules; the comment period closed 18 June 2026 and the proposals are not finalised.

title: Credit Risk Mitigation: Recognition Before Relief
one_screen: CR-07 → collateral mitigates loss severity; it does not replace repayment capacity. Regulatory capital goes one step further: economic protection reduces RWA only when the protection is eligible, legally effective and recognised by the applicable prudential method.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | CRM form | Prudential effect | | :--- | :--- | | Financial collateral | Can reduce recognised exposure after prescribed adjustments | | Guarantee / eligible credit derivative | Can substitute protection-provider treatment for protected amount | | Enforceable netting | Can recognise qualifying offsets instead of gross exposure | | Ineligible security | May reduce economic risk but gives no regulatory relief | The legal-enforceability test matters because capital relief assumes the bank can actually realise or call the protection when the obligor fails. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Front line / credit | Capture collateral and guarantee terms accurately | | Legal | Confirm enforceability and documentation | | Risk / capital | Apply eligibility and prudential treatment | | Independent assurance | Challenge data, legal opinions and calculation controls | ### Permanent rule Protection reduces regulatory capital only to the extent the capital framework recognises it. ### Never confuse [Economic mitigation] and [Regulatory CRM] **Economic mitigation** — protection that can reduce actual loss. --- **Regulatory CRM** — protection that also satisfies the prudential recognition conditions for capital relief. ### Permanent trap Subtracting every pledged asset's market value from exposure ignores eligibility, legal enforceability, haircuts and mismatch rules. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the principle. Eligible collateral, guarantors and detailed operational tests vary by jurisdiction.

title: CRM Mechanics: Substitution, Netting and Haircuts
one_screen: Once protection passes the eligibility gate, the capital calculation must use the right mechanism. Guarantees typically change whose credit quality drives the protected portion; collateral changes recognised exposure value; netting recognises enforceable offsets. Haircuts protect the calculation against value movement before close-out or realisation.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Protection | First calculation effect | | :--- | :--- | | Eligible guarantee | Substitute eligible protection-provider treatment on protected portion | | Eligible financial collateral | Adjust exposure and collateral values, then recognise residual exposure | | Eligible netting | Replace qualifying gross claims with prescribed net exposure | | Currency / maturity mismatch | Reduce recognition through prescribed adjustment | A haircut is not a predicted collateral loss. It is a prudential valuation adjustment for volatility, holding period, currency mismatch or related risk. A guarantee is therefore not "collateral with a zero haircut"; it follows a different risk-transfer mechanism. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Use the prudential mechanism that matches the legal protection; do not mix substitution and collateral-value adjustment. ### Never confuse [Haircut] and [Risk weight] **Haircut** — adjustment to recognised exposure or collateral value. --- **Risk weight** — factor applied after exposure measurement to determine RWA. ### Permanent trap Using the guarantor's risk weight for pledged securities simply because both are "security" applies the wrong CRM method. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the conceptual mechanics. Supervisory haircut tables, eligible instruments and national options differ.

title: IRB: Permission, Scope and Architecture
one_screen: CR-04/05/06 → PD, LGD and EAD are governed risk parameters. IRB allows an approved bank to estimate specified inputs for regulatory capital, but Basel still controls the asset classes, minimum requirements, parameter definitions and risk-weight functions. Internal modelling is permissioned prudential machinery, not a bank-selected alternative formula.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Foundation IRB lets the bank estimate fewer inputs; Advanced IRB permits more internal parameter estimation where the exposure class and local implementation allow it. Basel finalisation restricts advanced modelling for specified portfolios to reduce unwarranted RWA variability. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model development | Estimate permitted risk parameters | | Credit / rating owners | Operate ratings within governed processes | | Validation | Independently test model performance and limitations | | Capital function | Translate approved parameters into regulatory RWA | | Supervisor | Grant, condition, amend or withdraw permission | ### Permanent rule IRB means permission to estimate specified inputs inside a prescribed capital framework; it does not mean permission to set capital internally. ### Never confuse [Internal model] and [IRB permission] **Internal model** — bank-developed risk measurement tool. --- **IRB permission** — supervisory authorisation to use specified internal estimates for regulatory capital. ### Permanent trap Calling any PD scorecard an "IRB model" ignores the use test, governance, data, validation and supervisory approval required for regulatory use. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) **As at August 2026:** the final 2026 credit-risk Directions choose the Standardised Approach from 1 April 2027; IRB is not the new domestic commercial-bank credit-capital method. #### UK **As at August 2026:** Basel 3.1 IRB rules are final and commence 1 January 2027, with revised model-scope restrictions. #### EU CRR3 retains permission-based IRB subject to Basel-finalisation constraints and the output floor. #### US **As at August 2026:** the 19 March 2026 large-bank capital NPR is not finalised; its proposed expanded risk-based architecture is not a rule in force.

title: The IRB Risk Function
one_screen: CR-04/05/06 → PD, LGD and EAD measure different dimensions of credit loss; CR-10 → point-in-time and through-the-cycle calibration are not interchangeable. The IRB function combines regulatory parameters with supervisory maturity and correlation relationships to target unexpected portfolio loss, not merely expected loss.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Input | Capital intuition | | :--- | :--- | | PD ↑ | Default tail risk generally ↑ | | LGD ↑ | Loss severity at default ↑ | | EAD ↑ | Amount exposed at default ↑ | | Maturity ↑ | More time for deterioration can increase requirement | | Correlation ↑ | More common systematic tail risk | The mapping is nonlinear. Expected loss intuition such as PD × LGD × EAD describes a central expected amount under simplified assumptions; IRB capital adds the adverse systematic tail and regulatory calibration. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule IRB capital is a tail-risk calculation using prescribed supervisory structure; it is not PD × LGD × EAD. ### Never confuse [Expected loss] and [IRB capital] **Expected loss** — central expected credit loss. --- **IRB capital** — prudential unexpected-loss requirement generated by the regulatory function. ### Permanent trap Assuming a 10% increase in PD always causes a 10% increase in capital ignores the nonlinearity of the risk-weight function. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel mechanism. Local permission, parameter constraints and exposure eligibility determine where it can be used.

title: IRB Constraints and Specialised Lending
one_screen: Internal estimates are not allowed to fall without limit or to be used for every exposure.
