Basel constrains IRB through parameter floors, minimum data and estimation rules, exposure-class restrictions and, for qualifying specialised lending, a supervisory slotting route that classifies transaction quality rather than relying on an ordinary corporate PD/LGD treatment.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Specialised lending branch: Input floors operate before the risk-weight function. The output floor in CAP-19 operates after risk calculations at aggregate RWA level. Slotting is also different from an external rating: it is a prudential classification under the specialised-lending framework. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Regulatory modelling is bounded twice: first through model scope and input constraints, then through the aggregate output floor. ### Never confuse [Input floor] and [Output floor] **Input floor** — lower bound or constraint on a model parameter before the risk-weight calculation. --- **Output floor** — aggregate lower bound on model-based RWA relative to standardised RWA. ### Never confuse [Slotting category] and [External rating] **Slotting category** — supervisory classification of qualifying specialised lending. --- **External rating** — assessment issued by an eligible external credit assessment institution. ### Permanent trap Calling 72.5% a "PD floor" moves an aggregate RWA backstop into the wrong stage of the calculation. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the conceptual distinctions. IRB scope, parameter floors and specialised-lending implementation depend on local transposition and permissions.

title: The Output Floor
one_screen: The output floor limits how far approved internal models can reduce aggregate RWA below a standardised benchmark. The fully phased Basel calibration is 72.5% of standardised RWA; it is not a 72.5% exposure risk weight. **As at August 2026**, phase-in status is jurisdiction-specific and future steps must be read by date.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Example: Model-based RWA = 60 Standardised RWA = 100 Floor percentage = 72.5% Floor amount = 72.5 Binding RWA = 72.5 If model-based RWA were 80, the floor would not bind. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule The floor percentage multiplies the prescribed standardised RWA benchmark, not each IRB exposure. ### Never confuse [Output floor] and [Risk weight] **Output floor** — aggregate lower bound on model-based RWA. --- **Risk weight** — exposure-level or formula-derived scaling factor used within an RWA methodology. ### Permanent trap Applying 72.5% to every modelled exposure discards the aggregate comparison the floor is designed to perform. ### Jurisdiction variants #### UK (PRA) **As at August 2026:** final rules commence **1 January 2027**. The transitional multiplier is scheduled at **60% in 2027**, **65% in 2028**, **70% in 2029**, reaching **72.5% from 1 January 2030**. These are future phase-in steps under final rules, not proposals. #### EU **As at August 2026:** CRR3 is in force. The floor is **55% during 2026**, then **60% in 2027**, **65% in 2028**, **70% in 2029**, and **72.5% from 1 January 2030**. #### US **As at August 2026:** the 19 March 2026 large-bank proposal is not finalised. Do not teach a Basel output floor as an implemented US rule. #### IN **As at August 2026:** RBI has selected the Standardised Approach for the covered commercial-bank credit-risk framework effective 1 April 2027; an IRB-versus-SA credit output-floor mechanism is therefore not the domestic credit-risk architecture.

title: The Leverage Ratio Backstop
one_screen: Risk-based capital asks how risky exposures are; the leverage ratio asks how large the bank's exposure is relative to Tier 1 capital without ordinary credit risk weighting. Basel deliberately uses it as a simple non-risk-based backstop against model risk, classification risk and excessive balance-sheet leverage.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism The denominator is not simply total accounting assets. Basel includes prescribed treatment for on-balance-sheet exposures, derivatives, securities financing transactions and off-balance-sheet items. | Portfolio | Risk-based lens | Leverage lens | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | High-risk assets | Often high RWA | Exposure still enters denominator | | Very low-risk assets | May create low RWA | Still consume leverage capacity | | Model changes | Can alter RWA | Cannot remove the underlying exposure merely by lowering a risk weight | ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule The leverage ratio complements risk-based capital; neither can be inferred from the other. ### Never confuse [Total assets] and [Leverage exposure measure] **Total assets** — accounting balance-sheet quantity. --- **Leverage exposure measure** — regulatory denominator including prescribed on- and off-balance-sheet exposures. ### Permanent trap Using accounting assets as an exact denominator omits derivative, securities-financing and off-balance-sheet measurement rules. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) **As at August 2026:** RBI's 2025 capital directions prescribe **4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other covered commercial banks**. This position is in force. #### UK, EU, US Local leverage frameworks and overlays apply by firm category. The permanent concept is the same; exact requirements must be read from the live domestic rulebook.

title: Three Pillars, One Capital Architecture
one_screen: The three Basel pillars answer different questions. Pillar 1 asks what prescribed quantitative minimum follows from the rulebook; Pillar 2 asks what material risk and vulnerability that minimum does not fully capture; Pillar 3 asks what must be disclosed so outsiders can assess the prudential position. Buffers are not a fourth pillar: they sit above capital requirements.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Question | Output | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Pillar 1 | What do prescribed capital formulas require? | Minimum risk-based capital | | Pillar 2 | What risks or weaknesses remain insufficiently captured? | Internal assessment, supervisory review and possible additional capital | | Buffers | How much usable CET1 should sit above requirements for conservation, cycle or systemic risk? | Additional CET1 cushion | | Pillar 3 | What must market participants be able to observe? | Regulatory disclosures | The exact legal order and labels differ locally, but the conceptual error to avoid is treating Pillar 1, Pillar 2 and buffers as three interchangeable topics. Pillar 1 is the baseline calculation; Pillar 2 is the completeness check; buffers are deliberately usable layers above requirements. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Pillar 3 discloses the capital architecture; it does not itself add a capital layer. ### Never confuse [Pillar 2] and [Capital buffer] **Pillar 2** — institution-specific assessment and supervisory response to residual risks or weaknesses. --- **Capital buffer** — CET1 cushion maintained above applicable capital requirements for a defined macroprudential or conservation purpose. ### Permanent trap Saying "Pillar 1 + Pillar 2 + Pillar 3 = total capital requirement" wrongly turns disclosure into capital and ignores buffers. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel conceptual architecture. Domestic law determines the exact Pillar 2 instruments, buffer order and disclosure implementation.

title: Pillar 1: Minimum Risk-Based Capital
one_screen: Pillar 1 converts prescribed risk measurement into minimum capital requirements. It is deliberately standardised enough to be comparable across banks, but it is not intended to describe every risk that could threaten a particular institution.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Under the Basel global standard, before buffers, the minimum ratios are: | Ratio | Basel minimum | | :--- | ---: | | CET1 / RWA | 4.5% | | Tier 1 / RWA | 6.0% | | Total Capital / RWA | 8.0% | These are nested quality requirements. The 8% Total Capital requirement includes the capital already satisfying the CET1 and Tier 1 minima; it is not an additional 8% on top of them. Pillar 1 also depends on the permitted approaches used to generate RWA. Standardised approaches create common benchmarks; internal-model approaches may be permitted for specified risks and exposures subject to constraints. ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Pillar 1 is the common quantitative baseline, not proof that the bank has enough capital for every material risk. ### Never confuse [Basel minimum] and [Bank's binding requirement] **Basel minimum** — international standard agreed by BCBS members. --- **Bank's binding requirement** — requirement under its jurisdictional rulebook plus applicable firm-specific decisions. ### Permanent trap Quoting 8% as the bank's full required capital ignores CET1 quality constraints, Pillar 2, buffers and higher local minima. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the conceptual role. Numerical binding minima can differ materially; India is a clear example in CAP-29.

title: Pillar 2: ICAAP, Supervisory Review and Add-ons
one_screen: Pillar 2 is the completeness check on Pillar 1. ICAAP is management's disciplined argument that the bank's capital is adequate for its actual risk profile and strategy; supervisory review independently tests that argument and can require remediation or capital above the minimum.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Typical Pillar 2 concerns include concentration, interest-rate risk in the banking book, weaknesses in governance or risk management, model limitations and risks that are material but not fully captured by Pillar 1. The order prevents double counting: identify the risk, identify the Pillar 1 coverage already present, then assess the residual. Pillar 2 is not a generic percentage added because "Pillar 1 is conservative". ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Produces / owns | | :--- | :--- | | Business and risk owners | Risk identification and credible management actions | | Finance / capital | Capital projections and resources | | Risk function | ICAAP methodology and challenge | | Board | Approves risk appetite and capital adequacy | | Supervisor | Independently reviews and intervenes | | Internal audit | Assesses governance and control effectiveness | ### Permanent rule Management owns ICAAP; the supervisor reviews it. Supervisory review does not transfer responsibility for capital adequacy away from the bank. ### Never confuse [ICAAP] and [Pillar 1 calculation] **ICAAP** — forward-looking assessment of overall capital adequacy for the bank's actual risks. --- **Pillar 1 calculation** — prescribed minimum capital methodology. ### Permanent trap Starting ICAAP with a desired capital percentage and inventing risks to justify it reverses the process. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the Basel principles. Local frameworks determine the legal form of Pillar 2 requirements, expectations and supervisory communications.

title: The Buffer Stack
one_screen: Buffers answer a different question from minimum requirements: how much CET1 should remain available above requirements so the bank can absorb stress before breaching the prudential floor? Conservation, countercyclical and systemic buffers have different triggers and purposes, even when they all add CET1.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Generic stack: | Buffer | Risk addressed | Typical character | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Capital conservation buffer | General ability to absorb losses above minima | Standing | | Countercyclical buffer | System-wide cyclical build-up of credit risk | Time-varying | | G-SIB / D-SIB or systemic buffer | Externality from systemic importance | Institution/system-specific | The exact legal stacking order can differ. What does not change is that a buffer is intended to be entered in stress before the bank exhausts minimum capital. That usability is why distribution constraints intensify as buffers are consumed. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A buffer is useful precisely because the bank can enter it before breaching minimum capital, with consequences designed to conserve resources. ### Never confuse [Pillar 2 requirement] and [Buffer] **Pillar 2 requirement** — capital required because Pillar 1 does not adequately capture a bank-specific risk or weakness. --- **Buffer** — CET1 cushion maintained above requirements for conservation, cyclical or systemic purposes. ### Permanent trap Calling every amount above Pillar 1 a "buffer" hides the distinction between required institution-specific capital and deliberately usable cushion. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN **As at August 2026:** RBI applies a 2.5% CET1 capital conservation buffer above domestic minimum ratios, plus applicable countercyclical and systemic requirements. #### UK / EU **As at August 2026:** combined-buffer structures and firm-specific Pillar 2 arrangements follow local rules. The UK SDDT regime is final but has a future commencement of **1 January 2027** for eligible firms. #### US **As at August 2026:** large-bank capital uses the existing stress capital buffer architecture rather than reproducing the EU combined-buffer stack.

title: Using the Stack: Distribution Constraints and Headroom
one_screen: Regulatory buffers are designed to be usable, but using them is not consequence-free. As CET1 falls from management headroom into regulatory buffers, restrictions on dividends, variable remuneration and other distributions conserve capital before minimum requirements are breached.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Management headroom is voluntary capital held above the regulatory stack to protect against forecast error, volatility, strategy execution and market expectations. It is not itself a regulatory buffer. Under the Basel conservation framework, the deeper capital falls into the conservation-buffer range, the greater the proportion of earnings that must be retained. EU and ordinary UK terminology commonly uses maximum distributable amount mechanics for specified distributions when the combined buffer is not met. The US uses a different stress-capital-buffer structure. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Entering a buffer is less severe than breaching a minimum, but it is not the same as having unrestricted excess capital. ### Never confuse [Management headroom] and [Regulatory buffer] **Management headroom** — internally chosen margin above the regulatory stack. --- **Regulatory buffer** — rule-based CET1 cushion with defined prudential consequences when used. ### Never confuse [MDA] and [Capital stock] **MDA** — maximum amount permitted for specified distributions under the applicable regime. --- **Capital stock** — amount of qualifying regulatory capital held by the bank. ### Permanent trap Treating the buffer as unusable because distributions are constrained defeats its purpose; treating it as free surplus ignores the conservation mechanism. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN RBI applies capital-conservation restrictions as CET1 moves through prescribed buffer ranges. #### UK / EU MDA-style restrictions apply under their respective ordinary combined-buffer frameworks; exact calculations are jurisdictional. #### US Stress capital buffer rules produce a different large-bank distribution and capital architecture.

title: Stress Testing and Capital Transmission
one_screen: A capital stress test is a causal model, not a haircut applied to today's ratio. Scenario shocks change defaults, market values, revenues, expenses and balance-sheet behaviour; those changes affect both capital resources and RWA before the stressed ratio is recalculated.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Reverse stress testing runs backwards: Internal tests are bank-owned and tailored to the institution. Supervisory tests are authority-run or authority-specified and can support cross-bank comparison or formal capital consequences under local rules. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Risk | Scenario and risk transmission | | Finance | Earnings, balance sheet and capital projection | | Business | Credible behavioural assumptions | | Board / senior management | Challenge and action decisions | | Validation / audit | Independent testing of models and controls | | Supervisor | Challenge or prescribe supervisory exercises | ### Permanent rule A capital stress conclusion is incomplete until both numerator and denominator effects have been transmitted. ### Never confuse [Scenario stress test] and [Reverse stress test] **Scenario stress test** — begins with adverse conditions and projects outcomes. --- **Reverse stress test** — begins with failure and identifies conditions that could cause it. ### Permanent trap Deducting one loss amount from CET1 while holding RWA and earnings constant can materially understate stress transmission. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in the mechanism. Scenarios, governance, supervisory consequences and management-action rules vary.

title: Basel Standard to Binding Rule
one_screen: Basel is an international prudential standard, not a supranational banking statute. **As at August 2026**, the Basel Committee continues to set the common benchmark, while binding obligations arise through national or regional implementation. Every live capital question must therefore be dated and scoped before the formula is applied.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Use this workflow: 1. **Jurisdiction** — which legal regime applies? 2. **Status** — final rule, future final rule, proposal, consultation or guidance? 3. **As-at date** — what was true on the date being analysed? 4. **Commencement** — already in force or future? 5. **Scope** — which bank, exposure and consolidation level? 6. **Transition** — fully loaded or phased? 7. **Methodology** — standardised, modelled or special regime? Basel's Charter states that the Committee has no formal supranational authority and its decisions do not have legal force. Members commit to implement the standards domestically. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Never answer a bank-specific capital question from the Basel text alone when a domestic implementation exists. ### Never confuse [Basel standard] and [Binding rule] **Basel standard** — international benchmark agreed by BCBS members. --- **Binding rule** — domestic or regional legal requirement applicable to the institution. ### Permanent trap Saying "Basel is effective on date X, therefore every bank must use it on date X" ignores domestic transposition and transition. ### Jurisdiction variants **As at August 2026:** EU CRR3 is already substantially in application; UK Basel 3.1 final rules have a future 1 January 2027 commencement; India's revised SA and ECL rules have a future 1 April 2027 commencement; the US March 2026 capital package remains proposed after its comment period closed.

title: UK and EU Basel Finalisation
one_screen: The UK and EU share the Basel destination but not the same implementation clock or every implementation choice. **As at August 2026**, EU CRR3 has applied its main package since 1 January 2025, while the PRA's final UK Basel 3.1 rules are issued but commence on 1 January 2027.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Topic | UK — as at August 2026 | EU — as at August 2026 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Main status | Final rules; not yet commenced | CRR3 in application | | Main date | 1 Jan 2027 | 1 Jan 2025 | | Output floor in 2026 | Not yet operative | 55% | | Future floor | 60% in 2027; 65% in 2028; 70% in 2029; 72.5% from 2030 | 60% in 2027; 65% in 2028; 70% in 2029; 72.5% from 2030 | | Market-risk timing | FRTB internal-model approach from 1 Jan 2028 | 1 Jan 2027 treatment remains tied to the live delegated-act process | | Smaller-firm proportionality | SDDT simplified regime from 1 Jan 2027 | Separate CRR/CRD proportionality framework | The UK delay means its output-floor transition starts at the 60% 2027 step rather than replaying the EU's 2025-26 stages. For EU market risk, the Commission adopted a third FRTB Delegated Act on 4 June 2026; **as at August 2026** it remained under European Parliament and Council scrutiny, so the 1 January 2027 treatment must be read with that status attached. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Same Basel standard does not mean same current rule: commencement, transition, national choices and proportionality can differ. ### Never confuse [Final rule with future commencement] and [Rule already in force] **Final rule with future commencement** — final policy whose operative date has not arrived. --- **Rule already in force** — requirement currently applicable to the institution. ### Permanent trap Using the EU's 55% 2026 floor for a UK bank, or treating UK Basel 3.1 as already in force in August 2026, mixes implementation calendars. ### Jurisdiction variants #### UK **As at August 2026:** PS1/26 is final; main Basel 3.1 commencement is 1 January 2027; FRTB internal-model approach begins 1 January 2028. PS4/26 makes the SDDT capital regime effective 1 January 2027. #### EU **As at August 2026:** CRR3 is in application; output floor is 55% in 2026 with future annual steps to 72.5% from 1 January 2030. The third FRTB Delegated Act adopted 4 June 2026 remained under scrutiny; EBA material dated 3 August 2026 describes its application conditionally on entry into force.

title: India: Capital, Credit Risk and the ECL Transition
one_screen: India's binding capital ratios are not the Basel global minima, and its next credit-risk and provisioning changes share a commencement date but remain separate regimes. **As at August 2026**, current commercial-bank capital directions are in force; the revised credit-risk Standardised Approach and the new ECL provisioning Directions are both final but commence on **1 April 2027**.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Item | India position as at August 2026 | | :--- | :--- | | CET1 minimum | 5.5% of RWA | | Tier 1 minimum | 7.0% of RWA | | Total Capital minimum | 9.0% of RWA | | Capital conservation buffer | 2.5% CET1 | | Leverage ratio | 4% for D-SIBs; 3.5% for other covered commercial banks | | Revised banking-book credit-risk approach | Final Standardised Approach; effective 1 Apr 2027 | | New ECL provisioning framework | Final Directions; effective 1 Apr 2027 | | ECL transition relief | Optional declining CET1 add-back through FY 2030-31 | These are separate questions: RBI has explicitly selected the Standardised Approach for the revised commercial-bank credit-risk framework. IRB should therefore be taught as international architecture, not as India's new domestic method. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Do not substitute Basel minima, IRB or accounting rules from another jurisdiction for RBI's binding commercial-bank directions. ### Never confuse [RBI credit-risk SA] and [RBI ECL framework] **RBI credit-risk SA** — prudential methodology for banking-book credit RWA. --- **RBI ECL framework** — provisioning and income-recognition regime measuring loss allowances. ### Permanent trap Saying "ECL lowers RWA" confuses the provisioning regime with the risk-weight framework; ECL primarily affects carrying amounts, earnings and CET1, while the SA separately determines RWA. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) **As at August 2026:** capital adequacy Directions dated 28 November 2025 are in force. The SA Directions, RBI/DOR/2026-27/397, and ECL Directions, RBI/DOR/2026-27/398, are final and become effective 1 April 2027. The CET1 transition fractions then step down 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 through FY 2030-31 and are nil thereafter.

title: United States: Current Architecture and the 2026 Proposals
one_screen: The United States must be read as a current rulebook plus live rulemaking, not as an implemented Basel-finalisation package. **As at August 2026, three notices of proposed rulemaking issued on 19 March 2026 remain proposals: comments closed 18 June 2026 and none has been finalised.**
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Binding position: | NPR | Federal Reserve docket | Status as at August 2026 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Category I/II firms, significant trading activity, optional adoption | R-1887 | Proposed; comments closed 18 Jun 2026; not finalised | | Regulatory capital and standardised RWA | R-1888 | Proposed; comments closed 18 Jun 2026; not finalised | | GSIB surcharge and FR Y-15 | R-1889 | Proposed; comments closed 18 Jun 2026; not finalised | The three NPRs address large-bank and market-risk capital, broader standardised capital treatment, and the GSIB surcharge respectively. None replaces current rules before finalisation and an effective or compliance date. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A notice of proposed rulemaking is not a binding capital rule, even after its comment period closes. ### Never confuse [Comment period closed] and [Rule finalised] **Comment period closed** — the scheduled public-comment window has ended. --- **Rule finalised** — agencies have issued a final rule, normally with an effective or compliance date. ### Permanent trap Teaching R-1887, R-1888 or R-1889 as "the US Basel rule" as at August 2026 converts unsettled proposals into law. ### Jurisdiction variants #### US **As at August 2026:** all three NPRs were issued 19 March 2026; comments closed 18 June 2026; none is finalised. Current binding requirements therefore remain the existing US capital, leverage, stress-capital-buffer and applicable GSIB-surcharge framework until changed by final rule.

title: Obligor, borrower and counterparty
one_screen: Credit risk attaches to a person that owes performance, not to a customer label. **Obligor** identifies the legal or natural person responsible for the credit obligation; **borrower** and **counterparty** describe roles that may coincide with the obligor but need not.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What it means | Why credit risk cares | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Obligor | Person contractually responsible for an obligation | Default status and wholesale borrower risk normally attach here | | Borrower | Person receiving or using borrowed funds | Often the obligor in loans; not a safe synonym in every structure | | Counterparty | Other contractual party to a transaction | Central for derivatives, securities financing and settlement exposures | | Commercial customer | Relationship-management label | May contain several legal obligors and therefore several credit risks | One corporate group can contain several obligors. One obligor can have many facilities. A derivative counterparty can create a credit exposure whose amount changes with market value even though no conventional loan exists. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Front office / onboarding establishes legal identity and contractual roles | | Approves | Credit / legal functions confirm the risk-bearing entity and structure | | Consumes | Underwriting, limits, modelling, collections, capital and reporting | | Challenges | Independent risk, legal, compliance and audit test entity mapping and aggregation | ### Permanent rule Credit risk must be mapped to the legal or natural person responsible for the obligation before ratings, defaults, limits or exposures are aggregated. ### Never confuse [Obligor] and [Counterparty] **Obligor** — the person responsible for a credit obligation. --- **Counterparty** — the other party to a transaction; the term describes the transactional relationship and may or may not coincide with a loan borrower. ### Permanent trap Using “customer”, “borrower”, “obligor” and “counterparty” as database synonyms can propagate one entity’s rating, default or limit status to legally separate persons. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Legal definitions and regulatory wording vary, but identifying the person responsible for an obligation is universal.

title: Product, facility and account
one_screen: A product is a reusable lending design, a facility is a specific contractual grant of credit, and an account is an operational record used to book and service activity. Credit risk measures become ambiguous unless they declare which level they attach to.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Level | Owns | Typical examples of fields | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Product | Reusable commercial design | Product type, standard terms, target segment | | Facility | Actual contractual credit availability | Limit, currency, maturity, repayment schedule, covenants, security | | Account | Operational booking and servicing | Balance, postings, due dates, arrears, interest, fees | | Obligor | Person responsible for obligations | Rating, default state, aggregate limits | A simple term loan may be one facility with one account. A revolving facility can have several operational accounts. One obligor can hold facilities with different collateral, seniority and drawdown behaviour even when a common obligor PD is used. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Every risk measure must state its level: product, facility, account, obligor or a defined aggregate. ### Never confuse [Facility] and [Account] **Facility** — the contractual grant or commitment of credit, including its limit and terms. --- **Account** — the operational record through which balances, payments and arrears are booked; one facility need not equal one account. ### Permanent trap Treating an account-level delinquency flag as automatically equivalent to an obligor-level credit state can misclassify other facilities when the governing default framework applies a different propagation rule. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Regulatory rules differ on when account or facility events propagate to an obligor, but the object hierarchy itself is universal.

title: Exposure and aggregation levels
one_screen: Exposure is the amount or value subject to credit loss for a stated purpose; it is not automatically today’s drawn balance. The same relationship can produce different valid exposure numbers at account, facility, obligor, connected-group and portfolio levels.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Level | Question answered | What may be included | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Account | What is booked here now? | Outstanding principal, accrued items | | Facility | What credit position belongs to this contract? | Drawn amount plus relevant undrawn or contingent exposure | | Obligor | How much depends on this legal person? | Relevant facilities to the same obligor | | Connected group | How much depends on one linked economic risk? | Exposures to connected counterparties | | Portfolio | How much exposure exists across the book? | All included obligors/groups under the chosen perimeter | Funded and non-funded positions can both create credit exposure. A commitment or guarantee may have little or no current loan balance while still creating future or contingent loss potential. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Every exposure number requires both a **measurement basis** and an **aggregation level**. ### Never confuse [Outstanding balance] and [Exposure] **Outstanding balance** — the amount currently booked as drawn or owed. --- **Exposure** — the amount relevant to a stated credit-risk question; it can include future drawings, contingent claims or aggregation above account level. ### Permanent trap Setting exposure equal to current drawn balance for revolving or committed facilities can omit the amount that may be drawn or become due before default. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) The RBI Commercial Banks IRACP Directions define exposure to include funded and non-funded exposures, including underwriting and similar commitments. #### UK (PRA) Detailed regulatory exposure values depend on the applicable prudential approach; the conceptual distinction between booked balance and risk exposure does not change. #### EU CRR exposure-value rules vary by exposure type and credit-risk approach; the aggregation principle is unchanged. #### US US regulatory capital rules define exposure measures by asset and approach; current balance is not a universal substitute for exposure at default.

title: Connected counterparties and economic groups
one_screen: Legal separation does not guarantee independent credit risk. Connected-counterparty analysis aggregates persons when control or economic interdependence creates a common failure channel, so one concentrated risk cannot be disguised as several names.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Connection test | Core question | Credit consequence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Control | Does one person directly or indirectly control another, or are several under common control? | Treat connected exposures as one concentration where the rule requires | | Economic interdependence | Would financial difficulty at one likely cause funding or repayment difficulty at another? | Aggregate because apparent legal diversification is not economic diversification | | Mere commercial relationship | Are entities simply customers/suppliers without material dependency? | Investigate; do not aggregate automatically | Connection for concentration purposes is not the same as default propagation. Two companies can be aggregated for a large-exposure limit yet retain separate ratings and default statuses if the applicable default rules assess them separately. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Relationship teams and credit analysis identify ownership and dependency evidence | | Approves | Credit risk / designated governance confirms connected-group treatment | | Consumes | Limits, portfolio risk, regulatory reporting and capital assessment | | Challenges | Independent risk, compliance and audit test completeness and consistency | ### Permanent rule Count common failure mechanisms, not merely legal names. ### Never confuse [Connected counterparties] and [Single obligor] **Connected counterparties** — separate persons aggregated because their risks are linked by control or economic dependency. --- **Single obligor** — one legal or natural person responsible for obligations. ### Permanent trap “Same corporate group” does not automatically mean “same defaulted obligor”, and separate incorporation does not automatically mean independent concentration risk. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI’s Large Exposures Framework applies Indian prudential aggregation and limits to single counterparties and groups of connected counterparties; use the RBI framework in force for the reporting date. #### UK (PRA) PRA SS3/25 sets expectations for groups of connected clients using control and economic dependency concepts. #### EU The CRR large-exposures framework uses groups of connected clients and tests based on control and economic interconnection. #### US US legal lending-limit and aggregation rules use US-specific control/common-enterprise tests; they should not be assumed identical to the Basel connected-counterparty test.

title: Underwriting and the credit decision
one_screen: Underwriting converts information about the obligor, facility and environment into a governed decision to approve, decline or reshape credit. The decision starts with a sustainable **primary source of repayment**; collateral and guarantees can reduce loss if repayment fails, but they do not repair weak repayment capacity.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Decision layer | Question | Output | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Credit policy | What business and risk will the institution accept? | Target markets, criteria, limits, prohibited/exception cases | | Repayment capacity | From what recurring cash flow or resources will contractual payments be made? | Base-case debt service assessment | | Downside resilience | What happens if revenue, rates, costs or asset values move adversely? | Stressed repayment capacity and weaknesses | | Structure | Can tenor, amortisation, covenants, limit or pricing make the risk acceptable? | Proposed terms and controls | | Mitigants | What secondary recovery exists if primary repayment fails? | Collateral / guarantee assessment | | Approval authority | Who may accept this size, risk and exception profile? | Approve / decline / approve with conditions / escalate | A sound decision is not “good borrower versus bad borrower”. It is **borrower + purpose + amount + structure + repayment source + downside + mitigants + price**, all within policy and delegated authority. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Front office / credit analyst assembles facts, cash-flow analysis and recommendation | | Approves | Delegated credit officer, committee, senior management or board according to authority | | Consumes | Documentation, operations, monitoring, portfolio management and finance | | Challenges | Independent credit risk, second-line policy governance and internal audit | ### Permanent rule Approve credit primarily on sustainable repayment capacity. Treat collateral and guarantees as secondary protection unless the product is explicitly designed to repay from asset sale or liquidation. ### Never confuse [Credit policy] and [Approval authority] **Credit policy** — sets what risks may be taken and under what criteria. --- **Approval authority** — determines who may accept a particular exposure, size, risk or exception. ### Permanent trap A high collateral value can make an uneconomic loan look safe. If the borrower cannot service the debt, the bank has underwritten a workout, not a performing credit. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the core rule.** Local consumer-protection, responsible-lending, related-party and governance requirements vary, but sound underwriting universally requires defined criteria, repayment-capacity analysis and controlled approval authority.

title: Collateral, security and guarantees
one_screen: Collateral, security interests and guarantees are credit-risk mitigants only to the extent that the bank can legally rely on them and realise value when needed. Their underwriting job is to provide a credible **secondary way out**; their later LGD role is separate and depends on realised recovery cash flows.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Mitigant | What must be true | Main failure mode | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Collateral asset | Identifiable, valued, controllable and realisable | Value falls, asset disappears, sale is delayed | | Security interest | Validly created and perfected under applicable law | Priority or enforceability fails | | Guarantee | Legally effective claim on a capable guarantor | Guarantor lacks capacity or defaults with borrower | | Covenant / structural protection | Trigger and remedy are clear and monitorable | Breach occurs too late or remedy is weak | **Eligible value is not appraisal value.** A lending or risk value normally considers valuation uncertainty, volatility, liquidation time, prior claims, currency mismatch, concentration and policy/regulatory haircuts. ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Credit, legal, valuation and collateral-management teams establish evidence | | Approves | Credit authority accepts the mitigant within policy | | Consumes | Operations, monitoring, workout, capital and LGD estimation | | Challenges | Legal, independent risk, valuation review and audit test perfection and values | ### Permanent rule A mitigant is worth only what can be legally enforced and economically realised when the borrower is under stress. ### Never confuse [Collateral value] and [Repayment capacity] **Collateral value** — secondary recovery value available if repayment fails. --- **Repayment capacity** — the borrower’s ability to meet contractual payments from the primary repayment source. ### Never confuse [Guarantee] and [Collateral] **Guarantee** — a contractual promise by another person to perform or pay if the obligor does not. --- **Collateral** — an asset or property interest available to secure recovery. ### Permanent trap Counting a guarantee at face value without testing legal effectiveness, coverage and guarantor credit quality merely moves the credit risk to an unmeasured second obligor. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the economics.** Perfection, priority, insolvency treatment, valuation standards and regulatory recognition are jurisdiction-specific; production treatment must follow local law and the applicable prudential framework.

title: Default: defining the event
one_screen: Default is a governed credit state, not a synonym for arrears, loss, bankruptcy or write-off. Every PD, default rate, cure rate and LGD inherits the unit and events used in the default definition, so the event must be fixed before the metric.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Question that must be answered | | :--- | :--- | | Unit | Does default apply to an obligor, facility, account or retail pool? | | Event | Which qualitative and quantitative conditions trigger default? | | Materiality | Which past-due amounts are material enough to count? | | Propagation | Does one facility’s default affect other facilities? | | Exit | What permits return to non-default? | | History | Which date and state are preserved for modelling and recovery? | Basel’s IRB reference definition uses two routes for an obligor: **unlikeliness to pay in full without recourse to actions such as realising security**, or **more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation**. The routes are alternatives; later atoms own their mechanics. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Define default before measuring default risk, then preserve that definition across development, calibration, validation and reporting. ### Never confuse [Default] and [Loss] **Default** — entry into a defined credit-risk state. --- **Loss** — the economic or accounting shortfall arising from outcomes around or after default; default can still produce substantial recovery. ### Permanent trap Combining historical “bad” flags that mean 90 DPD, charge-off, bankruptcy or NPA creates a target variable with no stable economic meaning. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI commercial-bank asset classification is built around prudential **NPA** rules, not a word-for-word Basel IRB default definition. The IRACP Directions also cross-reference “default” in RBI’s stressed-asset resolution framework; mappings must state which definition is used. From **1 April 2027**, RBI’s 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions mandate an expected-credit-loss provisioning framework for commercial banks; that future provisioning regime does not make the Basel IRB default definition and RBI prudential classifications interchangeable. #### UK (PRA) The current UK framework remains CRR-derived. The January 2026 PRA SS3/24 version is **future policy effective 1 January 2027**, not the framework in force on 29 August 2026. #### EU CRR Article 178 uses UTP and past-due criteria. EBA’s May 2026 amended Guidelines have an **application date of 19 October 2026** and are future-effective on 29 August 2026. #### US Advanced Approaches rules distinguish wholesale and retail default definitions; specified retail categories use different mechanical thresholds.

title: Arrears, days past due and delinquency states
one_screen: Arrears measure unpaid contractual amounts; days past due measure how long payment has remained unpaid; delinquency buckets convert that clock into operational states. These are payment facts, not loss estimates or the complete definition of default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Measure | What it answers | Typical mistake | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Arrears | How much required payment is unpaid? | Treating amount as duration | | DPD | How long has the relevant payment been overdue? | Starting the clock from statement or month-end instead of due date | | Delinquency bucket | Which monitoring state does the DPD fall into? | Treating a bucket boundary as a universal default rule | | Out-of-order test | Is a revolving/OD/CC facility persistently irregular under its rule? | Applying instalment logic to revolving credit | DPD describes payment behaviour; the default definition determines when that behaviour, or separate qualitative evidence, becomes a governed credit state. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Calculate delinquency from the contractual obligation and the specified counting convention; do not infer default merely from an informal bucket label. ### Never confuse [Arrears] and [Days past due] **Arrears** — the unpaid amount. --- **Days past due** — elapsed time associated with an unpaid contractual obligation. ### Permanent trap Changing due-date logic, allocation of payments or day-end convention can create apparent credit deterioration or improvement without any change in borrower behaviour. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI requires overdue, SMA and NPA status to be determined through the day-end process for the relevant date. Its illustration moves a continuously overdue account to SMA-1 after 30 days, SMA-2 after 60 days and NPA after the applicable 90-day progression; OD/CC products use the defined “out of order” test. #### UK (PRA) Past-due status and materiality are inputs to the current regulatory default framework; arrears buckets used operationally are not themselves the complete definition of default. #### EU CRR/EBA rules distinguish days-past-due mechanics, materiality and unlikeliness-to-pay indicators; reporting past-due bands do not replace Article 178 default. #### US Different regulatory purposes and retail categories use different delinquency/default thresholds; there is no safe universal “90 DPD for everything” rule.

title: Unlikeliness to pay
one_screen: Unlikeliness to pay identifies default from the substance of credit deterioration before a delinquency clock necessarily reaches its backstop. It asks whether full payment remains likely without extraordinary recovery action; it is governed judgement, not a discretionary weakness label.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Evidence | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Repayment capacity deterioration | Can expected cash flow still service the obligation in full? | | Distressed restructuring | Would the borrower fail or suffer material difficulty without a concession? | | Credit-related write-down / sale loss | Does the bank’s own action evidence material deterioration? | | Insolvency / bankruptcy event | Does legal distress indicate repayment will be avoided or delayed? | | Security dependence | Is repayment only credible through enforcement or realisation of collateral? | A watch-list flag, downgrade or adverse news item is an **input**, not automatically default. Documented triggers and evidence standards prevent UTP from drifting across teams or cycles. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Relationship/credit monitoring identifies deterioration and evidence | | Approves | Credit risk or delegated default governance determines UTP status | | Consumes | Collections, restructuring, modelling, finance and regulatory reporting | | Challenges | Independent risk, model validation and audit test consistency | ### Permanent rule Assess UTP on the ability and likelihood to pay the credit obligation in full, not on how much the bank expects to recover after failure. ### Never confuse [Unlikely to pay] and [High LGD] **Unlikely to pay** — a default-likelihood conclusion about full contractual payment. --- **High LGD** — a severity conclusion about the size of loss conditional on default. ### Permanent trap Calling a fully secured exposure “not defaulted” because collateral should cover the debt confuses borrower repayment with recovery from security. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI commercial-bank NPA classification is its own prudential framework. Do not import a Basel IRB UTP label into RBI NPA reporting without an explicit mapping to the RBI rules in force. #### UK (PRA) The current UK framework includes unlikeliness-to-pay indicators. PRA SS3/24 provides the future Basel 3.1 expectations from 1 January 2027. #### EU UTP is an independent limb of CRR Article 178. The May 2026 EBA amendments apply from 19 October 2026 and should be treated as future-effective until then. #### US Advanced Approaches wholesale default expressly includes a determination that the obligor is unlikely to pay in full without recourse to actions such as realising collateral.

title: Past-due backstops and the 90-day rule
one_screen: A past-due backstop is an outer mechanical trigger, not permission to wait for the clock when earlier evidence already establishes default. In the Basel wholesale reference definition, UTP and more-than-90-days-past-due are joined by **OR**, not by a sequence requiring both.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism UTP trigger met first → Default now Past-due clock reaches applicable material backstop first → Default now Neither met → Continue non-default monitoring The backstop constrains optimism. It preserves an objective point beyond which prolonged material non-payment cannot remain outside default merely because judgement has not acted. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The backstop is the latest mechanical trigger under its rule, not a grace period that overrides earlier qualitative default evidence. ### Never confuse [Backstop] and [Definition of default] **Backstop** — an outer mechanical trigger based on elapsed delinquency under a specified rule. --- **Definition of default** — the full set of qualitative and quantitative conditions governing entry to default. ### Permanent trap Writing “default = 90 DPD” into data dictionaries suppresses early defaults, mixes products with different rules and trains models on a delayed target. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) For commercial banks, a term loan is classified NPA when interest and/or principal remains overdue for **more than 90 days**. RBI also prescribes distinct tests for OD/CC, working-capital irregularity, bills, agricultural exposures and other categories; asset classification is borrower-wise subject to specified exceptions. #### UK (PRA) The current UK CRR-derived default framework uses past-due and materiality rules alongside UTP. The updated PRA Basel 3.1 package, including the January 2026 SS3/24 version, takes effect on 1 January 2027. #### EU CRR Article 178 uses a past-due limb alongside UTP, supported by materiality rules. The EBA’s May 2026 amended Guidelines become applicable on 19 October 2026. #### US Advanced Approaches wholesale default includes more than 90 days past due on a material obligation, while specified retail categories use different mechanical thresholds; “90 days everywhere” is therefore wrong.

title: Restructuring, forbearance and distressed concessions
one_screen: Restructuring changes contractual terms; forbearance is a concession associated with the debtor’s financial difficulty. A modification can preserve value, but cannot erase the deterioration that made the original terms unsustainable.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Situation | Credit interpretation | | :--- | :--- | | Healthy commercial amendment | Terms change for ordinary business reasons; distress not implied | | Concession because of financial difficulty | Forbearance / distressed modification analysis required | | Material forgiveness or postponement | Test whether diminished financial obligation indicates UTP/default | | New contract after old arrears are capitalised | Preserve pre-modification history; do not reset the borrower to “new” | | Repeated restructuring | Escalating evidence that apparent cure may be unstable | The key question is **why terms changed and what risk the concession reveals**. Extending maturity may restore short-term affordability; capitalising arrears can clean DPD without improving cash generation; principal forgiveness changes expected recovery. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Workout / relationship team documents distress, proposal and economics | | Approves | Restructuring authority / credit committee approves within policy | | Consumes | Operations, finance, default management, modelling and reporting | | Challenges | Independent credit risk and audit test classification and economic substance | ### Permanent rule A new contractual schedule must not erase the borrower’s prior distress, default date or economic concession. ### Never confuse [Restructuring] and [Forbearance] **Restructuring** — a modification of contractual credit terms. --- **Forbearance** — a concession linked to the debtor’s financial difficulty; not every restructuring is forbearance. ### Permanent trap Evergreening converts unpaid amounts into a formally current contract while leaving repayment capacity unchanged; operational current status is not proof of economic cure. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Commercial banks apply the IRACP Directions together with the RBI *Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025* where relevant; restructuring classification and provisioning must follow those rules rather than a generic Basel label. #### UK (PRA) Distressed restructuring can be an UTP indicator under the definition-of-default framework; forbearance and regulatory default remain distinct classifications. #### EU CRR/EBA rules distinguish forbearance, non-performing exposure and default. The May 2026 EBA amendment retains the 1% NPV-loss threshold in the relevant distressed-restructuring guidance and becomes applicable on 19 October 2026. #### US Accounting modification, troubled-credit treatment and regulatory default are separate determinations; Advanced Approaches default remains governed by 12 CFR Part 217.

title: Cure, probation and re-default
one_screen: Cure is the governed transition from default back to non-default after the default conditions have ceased and renewed performance is credible. Re-default is a later return to default; a temporary payment or zero-DPD snapshot is not enough to prove a durable cure.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Default ↓ Original trigger ceases ↓ Required arrears / viability conditions met ↓ Probation or observation requirement, where applicable ↓ Cured / non-default ↓ New qualifying trigger? ↓ Re-default A sound data model keeps the entire state history: first default date, cause, restructuring events, cure date, probation, re-default and recovery. Deleting default history after cure produces survivorship bias and makes weak restructurings look successful. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Cure removes the current default state; it does not remove the historical fact that default occurred. ### Never confuse [Cure] and [Arrears clearance] **Cure** — return to non-default under the complete exit criteria. --- **Arrears clearance** — payment of overdue amounts; UTP or other default conditions may still remain. ### Permanent trap Resetting a cured customer to “never defaulted” inflates apparent portfolio quality and corrupts PD, transition and restructuring-performance analysis. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Under the current commercial-bank IRACP Directions, an NPA may be upgraded to standard only when the **entire arrears of interest and principal are paid**; where the borrower has more than one facility with the bank, arrears across all those credit facilities must be repaid, subject to additional restructuring rules where relevant. #### UK (PRA) Return-to-non-default is governed under the current definition-of-default framework. The updated PRA SS3/24 sets the future Basel 3.1 expectations from 1 January 2027. #### EU EBA Guidelines govern return-to-non-default and probation concepts. The May 2026 amended version has an application date of 19 October 2026, so the applicable version must be identified by observation date. #### US Advanced Approaches rules provide return-from-default standards for wholesale obligors and retail exposures under the US framework; the relevant unit must be preserved.

title: Write-off, recovery and economic loss
one_screen: Write-off changes the carrying amount or prudential treatment of an exposure; recovery records value collected after credit failure; economic loss measures what was ultimately lost after recoveries, costs and timing. None of these events should erase the default lifecycle that produced them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Lifecycle item | What it means | What must stay in history | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Default | Governed credit state begins | Default date, trigger, EAD | | Provision / allowance | Loss is recognised or reserved under the applicable framework | Amount, basis, date | | Write-off / charge-off | Carrying amount is reduced or removed under relevant rules | Written-off amount and date | | Recovery | Cash or value is collected after default/write-off | Gross proceeds, source and timing | | Workout cost | Legal, collection, maintenance and disposal costs | Cash outflow and timing | | Economic loss | Net shortfall measured on a consistent basis | Final discounted loss calculation | Post-write-off recoveries are economically real. A technical write-off can coexist with continuing collection activity and legal liability; the database therefore needs both accounting status and recovery status. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Never delete default, write-off or post-default recovery history merely because the balance sheet carrying amount has changed. ### Never confuse [Write-off] and [Debt forgiveness] **Write-off** — accounting or prudential reduction/removal of carrying amount under the applicable framework. --- **Debt forgiveness** — release of the debtor’s legal obligation; write-off does not necessarily produce forgiveness. ### Permanent trap Using the write-off amount as “LGD” automatically ignores later recoveries, workout costs, timing and the exposure actually outstanding at default. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) The commercial-bank IRACP Directions recognise write-offs, technical write-offs and subsequent recoveries. A partial or technical write-off does not permit the remaining exposure to be shown as standard merely because part has been written off. The current IRACP provisioning regime is replaced for covered commercial banks from **1 April 2027** by RBI’s 2026 expected-credit-loss-based Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions. #### UK (PRA) For IFRS reporters, IFRS 9 write-off requirements operate separately from prudential regulatory default. The two statuses must be mapped, not conflated. #### EU IFRS-reporting entities apply IFRS 9 write-off principles while CRR regulatory default remains a separate prudential state. #### US CECL allowance and charge-off practice is separate from regulatory default and nonaccrual classifications; modelling must preserve those distinctions.

title: Probability of default
one_screen: Probability of default is the probability that a defined obligor, facility or pool enters a defined default state over a specified future horizon, conditional on information available at an observation date. A number labelled “PD” is incomplete until its **unit, event, horizon and conditioning information** are known.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Required statement | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Unit | Obligor, facility or homogeneous pool | Changes what can default | | Event | Regulatory default, internal default or other defined target | Changes the outcome being predicted | | Horizon | One year, 12 months, lifetime or another period | Changes probability mechanically | | Observation date | Information available at prediction time | Prevents hindsight and leakage | | Calibration basis | Mapping from score/grade to probability | Turns ranking into a probability estimate | PD is not a declaration that a named borrower “will default”. It is a probability assigned before the outcome is known. Across repeated comparable populations, realised default frequencies should be consistent with well-calibrated probabilities within sampling and cyclical variation. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule No PD is interpretable without its unit, default definition, horizon and observation date. ### Never confuse [PD] and [Credit score] **PD** — a calibrated probability of a specified future default event. --- **Credit score** — a ranking or predictive output that need not itself be a probability. ### Permanent trap Multiplying a raw score by LGD and EAD because the score “looks like a probability” creates a loss number with no valid probabilistic interpretation. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in probability mathematics.** Regulatory frameworks can prescribe different default definitions, parameter floors, horizons and calibration standards; those rules change the parameter specification, not what probability means.

title: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle PD
one_screen: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle describe how strongly a rating or PD responds to current versus cyclical conditions. They are conditioning philosophies on a spectrum, not synonyms for short-horizon and long-horizon probability.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Point-in-time tendency | Through-the-cycle tendency | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Current borrower information | High sensitivity | Greater emphasis on persistent characteristics | | Current macro conditions | More direct response | Temporary cyclical effects damped | | Rating migration | Typically more frequent through the cycle | Typically more stable through ordinary cycles | | Near-term risk monitoring | Naturally responsive | Can lag rapid cyclical change if used alone | | Long-run calibration | May still require long-run anchoring depending on use | Does not automatically satisfy any regulatory calibration rule | A one-year PD can be PIT, TTC-like or somewhere between. Likewise, a lifetime forecast can use changing point-in-time macroeconomic paths. **Horizon and cyclical conditioning are separate axes.** ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule PIT/TTC describes sensitivity to current and cyclical conditions; it does not by itself specify the PD horizon. ### Never confuse [Point-in-time] and [Short horizon] **Point-in-time** — strong conditioning on information and conditions at the observation date. --- **Short horizon** — a forecast interval; it says nothing by itself about how cyclical information enters the model. ### Never confuse [Through-the-cycle] and [Long-run average PD] **Through-the-cycle** — a rating philosophy designed to damp temporary cyclical movements. --- **Long-run average PD** — a calibration concept; averaging observed defaults is not by itself a TTC rating system. ### Permanent trap Calling a multi-year average default rate “TTC” without examining rating assignment, macro sensitivity and calibration confuses statistical smoothing with rating philosophy. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Supervisors and accounting standards may require particular calibration or forward-looking treatment for specific uses, but PIT/TTC remains the same conceptual distinction.

title: Loss given default and recovery rate
one_screen: Loss given default is loss severity **conditional on default**. Collateral and guarantees influence LGD only through legally available, economically realised recovery value; an appraisal at origination is therefore an input to recovery expectations, not the LGD itself.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | LGD driver | Effect on net recovery | | :--- | :--- | | Borrower post-default payments | Increase recovery | | Collateral sale proceeds | Increase recovery after priority and costs | | Guarantee proceeds | Increase recovery if guarantee is enforceable and guarantor performs | | Legal / collection / maintenance costs | Reduce recovery | | Delay to recovery | Reduces present value | | Seniority and prior claims | Determine how recovery value is shared | | Downturn conditions | Can reduce collateral prices and recovery capacity together | A simple `1 − recovery rate` relationship is valid only when recovery rate and LGD use the same exposure base, cash-flow perimeter, costs and discounting convention. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Measure LGD from the default event using a consistent exposure base and economically complete recovery cash flows. ### Never confuse [Collateral value] and [LGD] **Collateral value** — one potential source of recovery, subject to legal rights, priority, sale value, time and costs. --- **LGD** — total economic loss severity conditional on default across all recovery sources and costs. ### Permanent trap `LGD = 1 − collateral value / current balance` ignores pre-default drawings, borrower payments, guarantor proceeds, senior claims, costs, timing and collateral-value stress. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the economic mechanism.** Prudential frameworks differ in recognised collateral, supervisory or internal LGDs, downturn treatment, floors and discounting rules.

title: Exposure at default and credit conversion factors
one_screen: Exposure at default estimates or prescribes how much is exposed when default occurs, not how much is drawn today. Credit conversion factors translate undrawn or contingent amounts into exposure, making pre-default utilisation behaviour part of credit risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Facility component | Credit question | | :--- | :--- | | Current drawn amount | What is already exposed? | | Undrawn commitment | How much can still be drawn before default? | | Contingent item | What amount can crystallise into a claim? | | Accrued interest/fees | What additional amount may be outstanding at default under the chosen basis? | | Limit cancellation / draw-stop behaviour | How much future drawdown is actually possible? | For a fully drawn amortising loan, EAD can be close to expected balance at default. For cards, overdrafts and revolving commitments, distressed borrowers may draw further before failure, so current utilisation can materially understate EAD. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule EAD is anchored to the default event. Current balance is an input, not the definition. ### Never confuse [EAD] and [Current utilisation] **EAD** — exposure expected or prescribed at default. --- **Current utilisation** — amount drawn now, often expressed relative to the facility limit. ### Permanent trap Estimating revolving-credit loss on today’s balance while LGD is measured against default-date exposure creates a denominator mismatch and usually understates drawdown risk. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the mechanism.** Regulatory conversion factors, modelling permissions and off-balance-sheet exposure rules differ by jurisdiction and prudential approach.

title: Expected loss: PD × LGD × EAD
one_screen: `EL = PD × LGD × EAD` is a compact one-period loss decomposition only when the three inputs describe compatible default events, horizons, populations and economic conditions. The arithmetic is trivial; parameter alignment is the real mechanism.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Parameter | Role in loss | Alignment test | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | PD | Chance default occurs | Same default event and horizon as the loss measurement | | LGD | Severity if default occurs | Conditional on that same default definition and exposure basis | | EAD | Amount exposed at default | Measured for the same default event and population | For a low-PD loan, the most likely realised loss may be zero while expected loss is positive. EL is an average across possible outcomes, not a prediction that every individual exposure will lose a fractional amount. Dependence can hide inside the inputs. Revolving utilisation and recovery severity can both worsen around default or in recessions. Multiplying three independently estimated averages without considering their conditional meaning can therefore misstate the true expectation. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Reconcile event, horizon, population, observation point and valuation basis before multiplying PD, LGD and EAD. ### Never confuse [Expected loss] and [Most likely loss] **Expected loss** — probability-weighted average loss over the defined horizon. --- **Most likely loss** — the modal outcome; for many low-PD exposures it is zero. ### Permanent trap Combining a regulatory one-year PD, a lifetime accounting LGD and today’s balance creates a numeric answer whose components do not describe one coherent loss experiment. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) For covered commercial banks, RBI’s 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions mandate an expected-credit-loss provisioning framework from **1 April 2027**. **No delta in the probability decomposition.** Regulatory capital, accounting ECL and internal economics prescribe different parameter horizons, conditions and treatments; the same formula label does not make those calculations interchangeable.

title: Retail versus wholesale credit modelling
one_screen: Retail credit is usually managed through large pools of comparatively homogeneous exposures, making repeated statistical patterns powerful evidence. Wholesale credit is usually more obligor-centred because exposures are larger, populations are smaller and borrower-specific financial, structural and legal information matters more.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Retail tendency | Wholesale tendency | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Number of exposures | Large | Smaller | | Individual exposure size | Comparatively small | Often material | | Homogeneity | Higher within designed segments | Lower | | Primary modelling unit | Pool / segment / facility behaviour | Obligor rating plus facility analysis | | Data evidence | Repeated behavioural observations | Financial statements, sector, management, structure, expert judgement | | Default application | Can permit facility/pool treatment under applicable rules | Generally obligor-centred in Basel-style wholesale frameworks | “Retail = model” and “wholesale = judgement” is too crude. Retail systems still need policy, overrides and fraud controls; wholesale ratings can use powerful quantitative models. The difference is how much **repeatable population evidence** versus **case-specific information** can support the decision. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Choose the modelling unit and method to match the economic homogeneity, data density and materiality of the exposures. ### Never confuse [Retail modelling] and [Automated lending] **Retail modelling** — pool-oriented estimation using repeated observations with similar risk characteristics. --- **Automated lending** — an operational decision process; retail credit can include manual review, and wholesale credit can use automation. ### Permanent trap Applying a mass-retail scorecard to a small, heterogeneous set of large corporates creates apparent statistical precision without a genuinely comparable population. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the economic logic.** Regulatory definitions determine which exposures qualify for retail or wholesale treatment and can impose size, pooling or management criteria.

title: Application, behavioural and bureau credit data
one_screen: Application models use information available at or before origination; behavioural models use information generated after the relationship exists; bureau or credit-information data add externally reported indebtedness and repayment history. Their common discipline is **time**: only information genuinely available at the decision or observation date may enter the prediction.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Information source | Observation point | Typical content | Limitation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Application | Origination | Declared/verified income, financials, demographics permitted by law, requested facility | No future account behaviour exists yet | | Internal behaviour | Post-origination | Payments, utilisation, arrears, balance trends, excesses | Requires account seasoning and clean observation windows | | Bureau / credit information | External reported history available at observation date | Other obligations, balances, enquiries, repayment history | Coverage, reporting lag, errors and thin files | | Policy / affordability | Decision-time rules | Eligibility, repayment capacity, limits | Not itself a statistical score | A bureau score or internal score is not automatically a PD. It must have a defined target, population and calibration. A “clean” thin file is also weaker evidence than a long clean history: absence of observed problems can mean absence of observation. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A model may use only information that was available at the point in time at which the prediction is supposed to be made. ### Never confuse [Application score] and [Behavioural score] **Application score** — risk ranking from information available around origination. --- **Behavioural score** — risk ranking from subsequent account-performance information. ### Never confuse [Clean bureau] and [Strong repayment capacity] **Clean bureau** — no adverse event observed in the covered reported history. --- **Strong repayment capacity** — sustainable ability to meet future obligations from cash flow or resources; bureau history is only one input. ### Permanent trap Allowing later delinquency, post-decision bureau updates or other future information into an origination model creates target leakage and makes model performance look unrealistically strong. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the modelling logic.** Data availability, permissible variables, consumer rights, credit-reporting frequency and automated-decision requirements vary materially by law and jurisdiction.

title: Rating grades, master scales and migration
one_screen: A rating grade is a discrete class of borrower credit quality; a master scale defines the ordered meaning of all grades; migration records movement through that scale over time. A grade is not meaningful because it is called “4” or “BBB-like”—its meaning comes from assignment criteria, ordering, default boundary and calibrated risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Element | Owns | Test of quality | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Rating criteria | How an obligor is assigned | Consistent use of relevant risk drivers | | Master scale | Ordered risk states | Clear monotonic deterioration from strong to weak | | Grade PD | Probability attached to grade/pool | Calibration consistent with observed/default definition | | Override | Governed expert departure | Reason, authority and performance tracked | | Migration | Movement between grades | Stable state definitions through time | | Default grade | Terminal/default state for the relevant system | Aligned with governed default definition | A transition matrix counts or estimates movement from each starting grade to each ending grade over a fixed interval, including default. Migration separates a static stock of weak borrowers from a portfolio actively deteriorating toward those grades. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Rating model/process assigns and documents the grade | | Approves | Credit authority or rating governance confirms assignment/override where required | | Consumes | Underwriting, portfolio monitoring, pricing, capital and reporting | | Challenges | Independent credit risk, model validation and audit test scale performance | ### Permanent rule A grade must retain a stable, documented meaning if historical default and migration statistics are to remain comparable. ### Never confuse [Rating migration] and [PD recalibration] **Rating migration** — the obligor moves from one risk grade to another. --- **PD recalibration** — the probability mapped to a grade or score changes; the grade label can remain unchanged. ### Permanent trap Changing grade criteria and then analysing the old and new labels as one continuous transition history produces false migration statistics. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the concept.** Regulatory frameworks differ in rating-system granularity, approval, floors, use tests and validation requirements.

title: Vintage analysis and roll rates
one_screen: Vintage analysis follows exposures originated at similar times as they season; roll-rate analysis follows movement between delinquency or credit states. Both restore the time dimension that a portfolio snapshot destroys.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Method | Groups by | Compares | Best at revealing | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Vintage | Origination period | Performance at the same months-on-book | Underwriting/channel/cohort changes | | Roll rate | Current credit state | Next-period movement to worse, same or better state | Direction and speed of delinquency | | Snapshot | Observation date | Stock in each state today | Current composition only | A six-month-old cohort and a three-year-old cohort have had different time to season. Comparing their cumulative defaults on the same calendar date confounds credit quality with age. Vintage curves instead align performance at month 1, month 2, month 3 and so on. Roll rates answer a different question: of accounts now at 30–59 DPD, how many cure, stay, move to 60–89 DPD or default next period? Identical current delinquency stocks can therefore hide opposite future directions. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Compare like with like in time: equal seasoning for vintages, and fixed start/end states and intervals for roll rates. ### Never confuse [Vintage analysis] and [Roll-rate analysis] **Vintage analysis** — follows origination cohorts through account age. --- **Roll-rate analysis** — follows transitions between credit or delinquency states through time. ### Permanent trap A fast-growing young book can look safer than a mature book simply because many accounts have not existed long enough to reach default. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These are analytical methods; local definitions determine the delinquency and default states being tracked.

title: Concentration and diversification
one_screen: Concentration risk arises when too much exposure depends on the same name, connected group, sector, geography, collateral type or underlying economic driver. Diversification comes from genuinely different sources of loss, not from the number of rows, facilities or legal entities in a dataset.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Concentration form | Common failure source | Example diagnostic | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Single name | One obligor | Exposure / capital or portfolio share | | Connected group | Control or economic dependency | Aggregated group exposure | | Sector | Common industry conditions | Sector share and stressed sector loss | | Geography | Local economy / law / property market | Regional exposure share | | Product / collateral | Common underwriting or recovery mechanism | Product or collateral-type share | | Hidden factor | Shared commodity, customer, currency or funding driver | Factor mapping / scenario analysis | Ten equal exposures to genuinely independent obligors diversify idiosyncratic failure better than one exposure of the same total size.
