Banks require higher entry capital and stricter licensing; NBFCs have a lower ₹2 crore equity norm but face similar prudential norms scaled to their assets.  Because NBFCs cannot create money via demand deposits, their funding costs and leverage limits differ fundamentally from banks.
bodyText: In practice, an Indian bank is licensed under the BR Act and can grant loans (including overdrafts, credit cards) directly funded by deposits. NBFCs (except certain rare deposit-taking ones) cannot open current accounts or offer cheque books. They can only accept term/lien-marked savings deposits with restrictions, and they must invest most deposits in government securities (e.g. PBs keep 75% in SLR securities). Banks contribute to CRR and SLR at set ratios; NBFC deposit-takers have their own (lower) CRR rates and no CRR if non-deposit NBFC. NBFCs access RBI refinancing schemes (e.g. MSE financing, mortgages) but cannot borrow directly through standard bank routes like repo. Regulatory burdens also differ: banks need full Basel capital ratios and AML/KYC; NBFCs follow RBI NBFC Directions (now largely converging with Basel norms for larger NBFCs). NBFCs often face extra restrictions on leverage, lending (e.g. sub-limits on unsecured loans), and must maintain Asset-Liability limits. For example, only banks count as “scheduled banks” in inter-bank systems. Moreover, only banks have statutory liquidity injection roles (like government banking), whereas NBFCs do not. ### Permanent rule Banks are permitted to accept demand (current) deposits and to extend credit directly; NBFCs cannot accept current account deposits or create payment mechanisms. Only SCBs hold RBI-guaranteed deposit insurance and use CRR/SLR facilities. ### Permanent trap Treating an NBFC like a small bank. For example, assuming an NBFC’s deposits are instantly withdrawable (like a current account) – this is false. Also ignoring NBFC funding limits can lead to compliance errors (NBFCs must invest most deposits in govt bonds, etc.). ### Never confuse **Bank** — a licensed entity that can take demand deposits (cheque/savings accounts) and provide a full suite of banking services. --- **NBFC** — a non-bank financial firm that cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques; funding comes via term liabilities, and it is generally outside central-bank clearing. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI delineates banks (BR Act) vs NBFCs (RBI Act) sharply. NBFCs have limits (no current accounts, limits on deposits) not found in US/UK banking. **No delta.** The general difference that banks take deposits and NBFCs do not is universal. But India’s deposit cap rules (e.g. ₹100k for PBs) are local details.

title: Asset Classification and NPA Norms (IRACP)
one_screen: Banks must classify each loan into Standard, Sub-standard, Doubtful or Loss assets based on repayment delays. A loan becomes a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) when interest/principal is overdue for 90 days.  The Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRACP) norms require daily monitoring (stamping) of accounts, with more provisions for higher-risk categories.
bodyText: Under RBI’s IRACP rules, a performing loan is **Standard** if not exhibiting any default and is repayable according to agreement. If a loan shows “signs of weakness” (like late payments but repaying) it may be classified as a **Special Mention Account** (SMA) first (see next atom) before becoming NPA. Once overdue beyond thresholds, it is classified as NPA with subcategories: - **Sub-standard**: NPA < 12 months, or assets showing incipient credit weakness. - **Doubtful**: NPA ≥ 12 months, significant uncertainty about recovery (e.g. liquidation value < book value). - **Loss**: NPA essentially uncollectible and fully written off (may be identified on a continuous basis and written off). For practical purposes, RBI mandates the *90-day rule*: any loan (principal or interest) unpaid for more than 90 days is an NPA. In many exposures (e.g. credit cards) RBI requires monthly (or more frequent) couponing into NPA status by 90 days overdue. The classification is updated daily through stamping in loan accounting systems. Banks must provide (p ) as per IRACP. Standard assets carry minimal provisions (0.4% or 1% of outstanding depending on secured status). Sub-standard assets require a **minimum 15%** provision (further if unsecured). Doubtful assets require higher provisions (20%–100% depending on how long in the bucket and available security). Loss assets have 100% provision. These provisioning rates and classification criteria are laid down in RBI’s IRACP Master Directions (updated periodically). ### Permanent rule A credit exposure is an NPA if interest/principal is overdue for more than 90 days. Once an asset is NPA, it must be classified as sub-standard, doubtful or loss according to RBI’s IRACP guidelines, and provisioning applied accordingly. ### Permanent trap Delaying NPA classification beyond 90 days past due. RBI requires daily stamping; waiting months to mark NPA breaches guidelines. Also, underestimating required provisioning for substandard and doubtful assets is a common mistake – RBI’s table mandates at least 15% for substandard, with more if unsecured. ### Never confuse **Standard asset** — loan with no signs of default; provisioned at RBI’s base rate (often 0.4% or 1%). --- **Sub-standard asset** — NPA overdue <1 year; shows weakness; provision ≥15%. --- **Doubtful asset** — NPA overdue ≥1 year; high uncertainty; provision much higher (up to 100%). --- **Loss asset** — uncollectible; fully provided. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s 90-day NPA rule and IRAC categories are India’s regulatory norm; UK/US use 90 days too, but account aging and provisioning differ.

title: Special Mention Accounts (SMAs)
one_screen: **Special Mention Accounts (SMAs)** are categories for loans showing early warning signals of stress, before becoming NPAs. RBI defines three SMA levels by days past due or consistent irregular payments. SMAs ensure banks monitor these exposures closely.
bodyText: SMAs serve as a watchlist under RBI’s framework. When a loan installment is overdue for 31–60 days, it is an **SMA-0**. Overdue 61–90 days becomes **SMA-1**. Overdue 91–180 days is **SMA-2** (by then it is an NPA if >90 days). These buckets help banks report accounts approaching NPA status. For example, a loan 45 days past due is SMA-0. Any payment beyond 90 days makes it automatically NPA (substandard category). SMAs capture loans at risk of slipping: if a borrower is regularly late or temporarily stressed, the account is flagged as SMA even if NPA threshold not crossed yet. RBI introduced SMAs to improve risk monitoring and discourage “evergreening” accounts (extending new loans to cover interest on old ones). Banks must report SMA balances to RBI daily. Regulators use SMA data to assess sectoral asset quality and systemic risk. No additional provisioning is mandated for SMAs (they remain performing assets) but banks should increase watchful provisioning as accounts progress through SMA categories. When an SMA-2 account crosses 90 days, it is upgraded to NPA (sub-standard). Thus, SMAs act as intermediate flags. ### Permanent rule Accounts must be flagged in increasing SMA categories as soon as they cross due-date thresholds (31, 61, 91 days past due). This daily reporting is mandatory. ### Permanent trap Ignoring SMA flags or delaying them. SMA classification is not a choice; banks must stamp accounts promptly at 31+ days overdue. Treating a stressed loan as “still standard” before 30 days beyond due violates rules. ### Never confuse **SMA-0** — overdue 31–60 days (early warning, pre-NPA). **SMA-1** — overdue 61–90 days. **SMA-2** — overdue 91–180 days (immediately becomes NPA if not resolved) SMAs are *not* regulatory categories with prescribed provisioning; they’re managerial flags. Once past 90 days, any SMA becomes NPA (Sub-Standard asset). ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s SMA classification is used; similar watch-lists exist in some countries but not all regulators formalize 30/60/90 day buckets.

title: Provisioning Norms for Banks
one_screen: RBI’s norms prescribe minimum loan-loss provisions based on classification and security. Standard assets require low provisioning (often 0.4% for secured, 1% for unsecured). Sub-standard assets need at least 15% (further higher if unsecured). Doubtful assets carry higher provisions (20–100% depending on seasoning and collateral). Fully-provided Loss assets require 100% provisioning.
bodyText: For **Standard loans**, banks must maintain a floating provision. Current guidelines typically require 0.4% of outstanding for secured standard advances and 1.0% for unsecured standard advances. These may vary by loan type and are updated periodically. For **Sub-standard NPAs**, RBI mandates a **minimum 15%** provisioning against outstanding (additional for unsecured portion). For instance, a 15% provision is mandatory even if there is collateral; unsecured portion may require a higher rate (at least 25%). For **Doubtful NPAs** (NPA >1 year), provisioning depends on how long the asset has been in that bucket and realizable security. Schematically: - Less than 1 year in Doubtful: ~20% (subject to security coverage). - 1–3 years in Doubtful: ~50%. - Over 3 years in Doubtful: 100%. Finally, **Loss assets** are those considered unrecoverable; they carry 100% provision. Banks must also consider security coverage (loan-to-value) in computing the shortfall. RBI provides a detailed provisioning schedule in its IRACP directions. If collateral liquidation value significantly covers outstanding, banks can adjust provisions downwards (but not below minimums). All these rates are the **minimum** RBI requires; banks can and do often provision more (for prudence). The actual provisioning entries are critical for regulatory capital and profit. The RBI periodically issues circulars updating these percentages and classification rules (e.g. 15% sub-standard). ### Permanent rule Apply the RBI-prescribed provisioning percentages by asset class: 0.4–1% for Standard; ≥15% for Sub-Standard (more if unsecured); higher for Doubtful (up to 100% with aging). ### Permanent trap Under-provisioning. A common mistake is assuming low provisions suffice when assets slip into Sub-Standard or Doubtful. RBI’s table demands at least 15% on Sub-Standard, and up to 100% on old Doubtfuls. Also forgetting security cushion (banks must provision on the unsecured portion). ### Never confuse **Standard asset provision** — minimal (0.4%/1%), since loan is performing. **NPA provision** — much higher: e.g. 15% (sub-standard) or more (doubtful). ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s percentages are unique to India’s IRAC norms (see RBI master directions). Other countries have their own loss provisioning, but India’s 90-day definition and fixed rates are RBI-specific.

title: Restructuring and Resolution Framework
one_screen: Banks follow RBI’s restructuring guidelines when a borrower’s credit stress is resolved via concession. This includes Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR), 5/25 refinancing, and more recently, the Resolution Frameworks (RBI’s COVID-19 and MSME frameworks). Under these, an NPAs may be restructured (terms changed) and classified as Standard again if conditions are met. Special norms apply to ensure loans aren’t “evergreened” without justification.
bodyText: Restructuring allows lenders to modify loan terms (extension of tenor, interest rate cut, etc.) for a viable borrower under stress. RBI has periodically issued frameworks: e.g. in 2014–15 the CDR mechanism (mostly phased out), and “5/25” for infrastructure. Post-COVID, RBI issued Resolution Frameworks (2020-21) letting banks restructure specified stressed loans with a benefit of preserving asset classification (subject to strict criteria). RBI also had schemes specifically for MSMEs (e.g. Mudra loans) and one-time restructuring packages for legacy stressed sectors. Under RBI policy, when a loan is restructured, it can be upgraded out of NPA only if it meets specific performance criteria over a period. RBI’s circular in 2015 clarified that a restructured advance must perform for at least one year (or two quarters) after restructuring to be considered Standard again. This avoids immediate upgrade fraud. If those conditions aren’t satisfied, the account remains an NPA. When restructuring occurs, banks must increase provisions (e.g. a minimum 5% on restructured standard loans, rising on restructured NPA). RBI’s norms spell out extra provisioning for restructured assets. Also, restructured loans carry enhanced reporting and are tagged on balance sheets. RBI’s resolution frameworks now overlap with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). Banks can opt for IBC proceedings for large defaulters, or choose RBI’s guidelines for out-of-court settlement. Both routes have specific timelines and safeguards to protect creditors and equitable treatment of all lenders. Resolution under IBC requires strict timelines (270 days) and NCLT oversight. RBI’s preference is that viable debt should not require formal insolvency if banks can resolve it cooperatively. ### Permanent rule When loans are restructured, they remain NPAs until strict conditions (specified by RBI) are met. Absent that, the classification stays NPA even if payments resume. Upgrading only happens after sustained performance post-restructuring. ### Permanent trap Assuming a restructured loan is automatically ‘standard’. In India, a loan modified under a restructuring scheme must still run successfully for a mandatory period before being considered standard. Banks often mistakenly revert classification immediately. ### Never confuse **Restructured loan** — a loan whose terms are modified to help a stressed borrower. It may still be NPA; upgrading depends on post-restructure performance. --- **Write-off** — outright removal of an asset from books. (Covered next.) ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s circulars on restructuring (e.g. Resolution Frameworks) are India-specific. Other countries have workout rules, but RBI’s emphasis on performance post-restructure is a local regulatory detail.

title: Upgrades and Write-offs
one_screen: **Upgrading** means moving an asset from NPA back to Standard after the borrower cures delinquency. RBI requires strict criteria: the loan must be fully repaid for a mandatory period post-default (e.g. 2 successive quarters or 1 year) and provisions made. This prevents manipulating classification. **Write-off** is when a bank formally removes an asset from its books, fully providing for it. In India, write-off is a prudential (not tax) exercise: losses are absorbed only after thorough review, and even then such loans may be sold or recovered later.
bodyText: Upon successful resolution of an NPA (e.g. borrower makes good on arrears or loan is restructured), banks may upgrade the asset to Standard. RBI’s 2015 clarification mandates a “cooling period”: for a restructured account to be classified as Standard again, repayments must meet conditions (like no defaults for two quarters). Without that probation period, an upgrade is not allowed. This rule was highlighted by RBI when it cautioned banks against prematurely upgrading SME accounts in 2014-15. **Write-offs** occur when a loan is deemed unrecoverable. RBI allows two types: *prudential write-off* (for banks, as per regulatory guidelines) and *technical write-off* (often a bookkeeping exercise after 2 years of NPA, for income recognition, but banks continue recovery efforts). After prudential write-off, a bank can still pursue the borrower or recover via SARFAESI/IBC. A write-off does not necessarily extinguish the debt legally (banks still have claim on assets). RBI’s rules require certain conditions (security realization attempts, etc.) before prudential write-off. Many NBFCs (like some housing finance) have their own write-off timelines but must adhere to RBI’s broad norms. Practically, write-off reduces a bank’s taxable income (since provisions were already made) but is a regulatory decision to clean balance sheets. The outstanding balance after write-off may be reported as ‘Outstanding written-off assets’ for supervisor attention. Only after full write-off can a new loan be given to that borrower under banking laws. ### Permanent rule An NPA cannot be downgraded to Standard until RBI’s post-default performance period is satisfied. Banks may only write off loans after exhausting all recovery options and meeting prudential criteria. ### Permanent trap Improper early upgrade. A common error is reclassifying a restructured NPA as Standard immediately. RBI’s circular forces a waiting period – skipping it breaks rules. Another mistake is treating a write-off as forgiveness: even after write-off, banks pursue the borrower. ### Never confuse **Upgrade** — reclassification of an NPA to Standard after borrower cures. Requires RBI-mandated wait period (e.g. no default for 2 quarters). **Write-off** — formally removing the loan from active books (after full provision); often a tactical cleanup, but the borrower’s liability remains. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s detailed upgrade criteria are India-specific. Many jurisdictions similarly prevent immediate NPA cures, but RBI’s exact timelines (e.g. 2Q after restructure) are local.

title: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Targets
one_screen: Indian banks must lend a mandated share of their credit to specified “priority sectors” (agriculture, MSMEs, etc.) as defined by RBI, often 40% of net bank credit for domestic banks. Within this, sub-targets exist (e.g. farm credit, smaller loans, micro-enterprises, poorer sections). PSL quotas shape lending portfolios: banks issue loans just to meet these percentages and may sell excess obligation via certificates (PSLCs).
bodyText: Under current RBI rules, domestic banks’ overall PSL target is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (with RRBs at 75%). Within that, there are sub-targets: at least 18% to agriculture (including 8% to small farmers), 7.5% to micro-enterprises, etc. There is also a category of lending to weaker sections (10% of ANBC) and a target to small-scale industries (7.5%). Loans to export sectors, large industries, or corporates do NOT count. PSL has grown to cover new areas (education, housing, renewable energy) as per RBI prescriptions. Starting in 2016, RBI allowed banks that exceed PSL targets to sell Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) to others who fall short. This “bank-on-bank trading” ensures goals are met system-wide. PSLCs come in types – e.g. Agriculture, Micro, General PSL – reflecting the underlying loan category. Priority sector rules profoundly shape Indian bank books: banks fund many low-yield rural loans simply to comply with the 40% mandate. This constrains their liquidity and profitability (since many PSL segments demand concessional rates or higher risk). Unlike any developed-country system, India’s mandatory directed-credit framework ties national policy to banking regulation. ### Permanent rule RBI-prescribed lending quotas (e.g. 40% to PSL) are mandatory. Banks must ensure each year’s lending meets or exceeds these sub-targets. ### Permanent trap Ignoring sub-categories and PSL certificates. A bank might focus only on agriculture without meeting MSME or weaker section targets, risking non-compliance. Also, some assume PSL is optional – it is not. ### Never confuse **PSL quotas** — mandatory lending targets (40% of bank credit to certain sectors). **PSLC (certificates)** — tradable certificates representing excess PSL achievement; used to buy compliance. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — Mandatory priority-sector quotas are unique to India’s financial system. (No similar directed-credit rules exist under PRA/Fed/FASB.)

title: Priority Sector Categories (Agri, MSME, Weaker)
one_screen: The “priority sectors” comprise several categories. Key ones include **Agriculture** (direct loans to farmers, etc.), **Micro and Small Enterprises (MSMEs)** (business loans up to specified limits), and **Weaker Sections** (targeted small borrowers). RBI regularly revises definitions: e.g. what constitutes a small farm or loan limit for microenterprise. Understanding each is crucial since only these count toward PSL quotas.
bodyText: **Agriculture (18% target):** Loans to farmers (individual or joint) for agriculture and allied activities. This includes crop loans, agricultural equipment loans, irrigation loans, and loans to agri-related services. Within agri, there is an 8% target specifically for small and marginal farmers (holding <2ha). Also loans to agri corporations, horticulture, and some farm sector supply chain are included. **MSMEs (7.5% target):** Loans to micro, small enterprises (as per MSME Act definitions) for business purposes. Also very small businesses (like retail shops, crafts). Recently, RBI expanded the definition to include loans to MSMEs up to ₹5 crore (and with turnover criteria). Loans to larger SMEs (beyond ₹5 cr) are out of PSL. **Weaker Sections (10% target):** This is a portion of PSL loans to small borrowers: it includes small farmers, microenterprises, borrowers from marginalized communities, and loans up to ₹50,000 (whichever sector). Essentially, a subset of agri, micro, and other small loans targeted at the bottom of economic pyramid (ST/SC, economically backward, etc.). Other PSL categories include education loans, housing loans (to EWS/LIG segments), renewable energy, and loans to specific small-scale service industries. Banks must use RBI’s PSL guidelines booklet to classify loans correctly. Only loans falling in these categories count; e.g. a big corporate loan does not. Overall, PSL shapes balance sheets: banks often build rural branches and specialized MSME credit teams to meet these targets. Satisfied PSL requirements can improve regulatory standing (e.g. risk weight relief), while shortfalls incur penalties. As RBI notes, PSL fosters socio-economic goals but also forces banks into lower-yielding lending. ### Permanent rule Only loans to RBI-defined priority categories count toward PSL. Agriculture loans, small enterprise finance, and weaker section lending have separate sub-targets. ### Permanent trap Misclassifying loans. E.g., making a small business loan to an urban store and hoping it counts as agriculture PSL – it does not. Each category has strict definitions. Also, banks sometimes ignore the ‘weaker sections’ requirement thinking general MSME lending covers it – but weaker sections is a distinct sub-target. ### Never confuse **Agriculture credit** — includes crop/pump loans etc. (part of 18% PSL). **Weaker sections** — a subset of priority sector covering loans to marginalized and poorest borrowers, under the 10% sub-target of ANBC. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — These exact sectoral categories (e.g. the 18% agri target) are unique to India’s RBI framework. Other countries may have development lending programs, but not tied to bank quotas.

title: Digital Lending Guidelines (Platforms and KFS)
one_screen: In 2022–2023, RBI issued comprehensive norms on digital lending to protect consumers from predatory fintech practices. It defines *Lending Service Providers* (LSPs) who partner with banks/NBFCs to distribute credit via apps. Key requirements include issuing a mandatory *Key Fact Statement (KFS)* for each loan, ensuring loans are disbursed into borrowers’ bank accounts (no third-party “pass-through” accounts), and capping upfront fees. LSPs also must register with RBI and have grievance officers. These rules address mis-selling and hidden charges that were rampant in unregulated lending apps.
bodyText: The context: unregulated loan apps led to harassment and exorbitant rates. In Feb 2022, RBI’s Master Directions on Digital Lending standardized the space. **Lending Service Providers** (non-bank fintechs who process applications) must follow KYC standards, get Permanent Account Number (PAN)/Aadhaar, and have a formal tie-up with a bank/NBFC. Every digital loan app must display, before disbursal, a *Key Fact Statement* summarizing the rate of interest, all fees and charges (incl. late payment fees), total amount payable, EMI/tenor etc. This ensures transparency. Borrowers must consent to these terms electronically. **Disbursal and repayment:** Loans must be disbursed directly to the customer’s bank account or their PSP wallet. Use of any “pass-through” account (e.g. an agent’s account) is banned. Similarly, repayments cannot flow through third-party accounts: they must go to the lender directly. This severed the practice of routing funds through shell accounts. **Fee and guarantee rules:** Fintech LSPs often offered “first loss default guarantees” to banks (promising to cover initial losses). RBI clarified these are not true securitizations but credit guarantees, and capped them at 20% of exposure or INR 5 cr. Also, LSPs cannot charge any fee at loan start except as explicitly disclosed – no pre-check fees. **Grievance redress:** Digital lenders must list a nodal grievance officer. Any user complaint must be addressed per RBI’s turnaround times. Ombudsman schemes also cover digital loans. Unfair collection by aggressive agents is prohibited under the Recovery Agent Code (see Consumer section). The RBI guidelines distinguish digital lending as a mechanism: *the loan contract is between lender and borrower*, while LSPs act as technology intermediaries. This “platform neutrality” means fintech apps cannot circumvent banking norms – borrowers can always refer to the original lender’s terms. Overall, these rules aim for consumer protection without stifling innovation: licensed entities can still use tech for underwriting (including data analytics, Aadhar/KYC), but must do so under RBI oversight. ### Permanent rule Digital lending platforms must issue a clear *Key Fact Statement* before loan disbursement, showing all charges and repayment terms. Loans must disburse directly to the customer’s own bank/wallet account, and no pass-through accounts are allowed. ### Permanent trap Loan sharks often created tech “platforms” outside regulation. A pitfall is thinking a fintech app can lend on its own terms. RBI’s rules require the actual loan to be from a bank/NBFC with digital co-lending only. Also, ignoring the KFS requirement can lead to non-compliance – every loan must show fully loaded APR and fees upfront. ### Never confuse **Lending Service Provider (LSP)** — a non-bank platform or fintech that facilitates loan origination on behalf of a bank/NBFC. Not a lender itself. **Fintech loan** — an RBI-licensed lender’s loan disbursed via a digital channel. (Not simply “getting money from a random app”.) ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI was among the first to regulate digital lending apps directly in such detail (re: KFS, pass-through ban). In UK/US, digital lending is allowed but individual states or laws handle disclosures (e.g. Truth-in-Lending Act) differently, and there is no blanket ban on pass-through accounts.

title: Digital Lending: Flow, Guarantees, and Securitisation
one_screen: Beyond transparency, RBI’s digital lending rules impose strict flow-of-funds and guarantee limits. Loans must be disbursed directly, and repayments must go to the original lender. The RBI also defined and capped “First Loss Default Guarantees” (FLDG) by fintechs, clarifying these are not true securitisation. Any arrangement where an app provider keeps collateral or routes funds illegitimately is prohibited.
bodyText: A key mandate: **Direct disbursal and repayment.** Any credit extended via a lending app must be paid into the customer’s own bank/PSP account – no money passes through the fintech or any third party. Similarly, loan repayments (EMIs) must be paid directly to the bank/NBFC. This is to prevent misappropriation. RBI explicitly forbids any “pooling or sweep accounts” that were used by some apps to skim funds. **Guarantee arrangements:** Fintechs used to offer to cover the bank’s losses (FLDG) up to some amount to motivate banks to lend. RBI treats an FLDG (capping around 20% of loan principal or ₹5 crore, whichever lower) as a credit enhancement, not traditional securitisation. Such guarantees must be explicit and capped by contract. They differ from securitisation: in a normal securitisation, credit risk is split among investors and not guaranteed by originator. Under RBI’s regime, if a fintech guarantees 20% of a loan’s loss, that fintech is effectively retaining part of credit risk (so regulator counts only 80% transfer as securitization). These agreements must be disclosed to borrowers. RBI’s limit (20%/₹5cr) prevents full risk transfer in a grey-camouflage way. RBI’s guidance also affirms that a fintech providing FLDG cannot park consumer funds. If a fintech receives payment from a borrower (say for processing), it must immediately route it to the bank. Collecting money and redisbursing it later is not allowed. Essentially, the fintech’s role is only origination & tech; money flows directly between borrower and bank. **First Loss Guarantee vs. Securitisation:** RBI emphasises they are distinct. In a securitisation, the originator may sell a pool of loans (and risk) to investors; there is no party assuring losses beyond already sold tranches. In a FLDG, the fintech agrees to compensate the bank for first losses. Because the guarantee can distort borrowers’ incentives and hides the true risk, RBI caps and requires disclosure of FLDGs. A FLDG is treated prudentially – the lender must still provision if a guarantee is in place (it’s not risk-free). ### Permanent rule No “pass-through” accounts in lending: funds must flow directly between borrower and lender. Any first-loss guarantee by a fintech must be contractually capped (max 20% of loan or ₹5 cr) and is **not** a pure securitisation. ### Permanent trap Using agent accounts to disburse or collect loan money. Some apps tried to appear as platforms but routed payments through their own accounts — RBI now explicitly forbids this. Also, fintechs believing they can guarantee entire losses – RBI caps such guarantees. ### Never confuse **FLDG (First-Loss Default Guarantee)** — a fintech’s commitment to cover an agreed fraction (max 20%) of losses on a loan. This is a credit support, not full securitisation. **Securitisation** — selling loan assets and credit risk to investors (no partial guarantee by originator). ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s treatment of fintech guarantees (FLDG) as limited and capping them is specific. Other countries allow fintech partnerships but often regulate them case-by-case (e.g. US banking regs). No identical cap is universal.

title: Digital Lending Grievance Redressal
one_screen: RBI mandates that all regulated entities using digital lending have formal grievance mechanisms. Lenders and fintechs must appoint nodal officers for customer complaints. Borrowers must be informed of escalation paths (including Banking Ombudsman). RBI also requires that both lenders and their tech partners resolve complaints quickly, tracking them in regular reports.
bodyText: The digital lending directions specify that every app or digital lender must provide clear contact details for grievance redressal. This includes an official Nodal Officer name/contact who handles issues. If a borrower complains (overcharging, collection practice, etc.), the lender must address it as per RBI’s standard timelines (e.g. 3-4 weeks resolution). Firms must also publish details of the Banking Ombudsman scheme, since appellants can approach it if unsatisfied. Moreover, under RBI’s 2016 Outsourcing guidelines (augmented in 2022 for recovery agents), banks must ensure their fintech partners and any recovery agents follow proper conduct. Customers should not face harassment or 24/7 calls. If needed, the customer’s complaint to the lender can be escalated through RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme. Tech-savvy customers often get quick redress via email or app, but the requirement is to maintain logs of all complaints and resolutions. In effect, RBI’s digital lending rules tighten accountability. A startup cannot avoid RBI oversight by claiming to be a “technology platform” – it must still honor consumer protection rules. Consumers have the same rights (transparency, appeals) as with brick-and-mortar banks when dealing via an app. For example, if a fintech breaches RBI’s guidelines, the bank’s grievance cell must still be answerable. Some fintechs go further (e.g. fintech ombudsmen) but legally the RBI framework covers all. ### Permanent rule All digital lenders must publish and operate a grievance redress system. Complaints must first go to a designated Nodal Officer. The Banking Ombudsman scheme covers digital loan disputes. ### Permanent trap Neglecting offline complaint channels. Assuming “if it’s digital, complaints must be emailed” – RBI requires accessible contact points and escalation. Also, sometimes start-ups think only their tech side is liable, but RBI holds the actual NBFC/bank accountable for the borrower’s redress. ### Never confuse **Lending app support** — the platform or lender’s own customer service/email. **Banking Ombudsman** — RBI’s formal consumer forum. After exhausting internal redress, the borrower can approach it about digital loan issues (as with any bank). ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI specifically requires digital loan grievance offices. Elsewhere, similar tech-lending regulations are nascent; EU has Digital Finance proposals, but no RBI-style scheme yet.

title: Co-Lending Framework (Banks-NBFCs)
one_screen: In 2018, RBI launched a co-lending scheme where banks and eligible NBFCs jointly finance borrowers. Under this, the bank must retain at least 20% of each co-lent loan portfolio (even if the NBFC originated most). Typically, the bank holds the larger share (say 80%) to keep better assets. The NBFC services the loan (e.g. documentation, collection) while sharing credit risk. Co-lending requires both parties to reconcile accounts and operations carefully, since each one-on-one partnership involves dual loan accounts and revenue splits.
bodyText: Under the *Co-Lending Model* (CoL), a bank and an NBFC enter a formal agreement. They extend credit to a common borrower at a predetermined ratio. One pattern is 80:20 (bank:NBFC) or 70:30, but RBI’s 2023 updates mandate minimum bank share of 20% for this scheme. In practice, many big banks take 80% and partner with smaller NBFCs (especially MFIs) that originate and service the loan to micro customers. All documentation must be in both names, and collections are shared. For example, the bank provides funds to NBFC (or directly to borrower), but NBFC handles field appraisal. The repayments are then split per the agreed ratio. This model aims to leverage NBFC outreach (last-mile distribution, quick appraisals) while giving banks a strong share of safer assets. Both parties must decide upfront on interest rate split, service fees to NBFC, and NPA handling. Operationally, co-lending adds complexity: two sets of ledgers (bank’s book and NBFC’s), reconciliation of cashflows, dual KYC checks, etc. If a borrower defaults, both share the loss per their ratio. RBI requires co-lending accounts to be reported correctly in their prudential returns (assets doubled: one on each book). Tax and accounting rules also reflect that a co-lent loan is partly a loan to NBFC (on bank book) and partly bank’s loan to borrower. The CoL framework was revised: initially introduced in 2018, it was formalized by Master Directions in 2021 and updated in 2023. The 2023 revision relaxed some earlier restrictions (like making NBFC proportion flexible up to 80%). It also allowed banks to lend their own share through partnerships (bank fraction can be higher). These policies aim to expand affordable credit (especially to underserved borrowers of NBFCs) by leveraging bank deposit base. ### Permanent rule In any RBI-approved co-lending arrangement, the bank must retain at least 20% (and typically holds the majority) of the credit amount. Both parties share risk and ownership accordingly. ### Permanent trap Misunderstanding who owns the loan: both do. A common mistake is booking the entire amount on one balance sheet; instead, each books its share. Also, forgetting that two payment schedules exist – banks must get their share. ### Never confuse **Co-lending** — joint financing by bank + NBFC on a single loan to a borrower. Each funds part (min. 20% by bank) and shares title. --- **Syndication** — multiple banks lending separate portions to one borrower, each with own loan. (Co-lending keeps one loan, two lenders, not a consortium of loans.) ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s co-lending model is unique (though other countries have bank–nonbank partnerships, they are usually simpler).

title: Co-Lending Operations and Reconciliation
one_screen: Practically, co-lending requires careful accounting on both sides. Each co-lending loan is reflected twice: a fraction on the bank’s books and the complementary on the NBFC’s books. Collections and disbursements must be reconciled to ensure each partner receives exactly its share. Often, the NBFC handles origination and collection (sometimes via its own BC network), remitting the bank’s portion of principal and interest as per the agreed split. The complexity of dual servicing and settlement is where most co-lending operations focus.
bodyText: Consider a ₹10 lakh loan co-lent at 80:20. The bank disburses ₹8L (possibly via the NBFC’s escrow), and the NBFC ₹2L. The NBFC may use its credit underwriting. When the borrower repays, the NBFC collects full EMI and must immediately allocate ₹8 of every ₹10 repayment to the bank’s account. RBI requires this flow to be documented, often via escrow or trustee arrangements. Both lenders then account: the bank books ₹8L asset, NBFC books ₹2L asset (showing ₹8L as a loan to NBFC if it was an advance). Reconciling these transactions is crucial each month. Banks and NBFCs often have joint MIS (Management Information System) to track co-lending pools. Differences (timing, rounding) must be resolved, or interest mismatches occur. RBI guidelines mandate that co-lending contracts clearly define default risk-sharing: if the borrower defaults, the bank and NBFC write off the respective shares in NPA. The NBFC’s share is often fully provided since the borrower mostly owes NBFC’s smaller part last (depending on waterfall, if any). Operational burdens include dual KYC process (both lenders verify the borrower), dual documentation, and regulatory reporting. For example, both lenders report their part of the loan in returns (one sees an inter-company advance, the other the borrower advance). Oversight demands that both sides have audit rights and controls over the loan pool. Despite the paperwork, co-lending is encouraged because it leverages NBFC outreach while using cheaper bank funds. Analysts must however note that it creates many micro-contractual relationships. Staff in banks and NBFCs must ensure cash flows match contractual splits exactly – failure can lead to compliance flags (like undisclosed bridging finance if the NBFC temporarily covers the bank’s share). ### Permanent rule Each co-lent account must be recognized on both the bank’s and NBFC’s balance sheets in the agreed ratio. Collections must be split immediately per that ratio. ### Permanent trap Neglecting reconciliation: assuming the NBFC’s collection is the end. In fact, the bank’s share must be remitted precisely each payment cycle. Failing to transfer promptly can violate regulations and trigger funding issues. ### Never confuse **Disbursement ratio** — split of funds lent (e.g. bank:NBFC 80:20). **Risk ratio** — same as disbursement split (each bears losses in proportion). These two are identical in RBI’s co-lending rules. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — Such formal bank-NBFC co-lending (with a fixed 20% bank retention) is currently unique.

title: Account Aggregators and GST Data in Lending
one_screen: The Account Aggregator (AA) ecosystem enables customers to share financial data from banks, investments and tax (GST) authorities with lenders upon consent. An AA is an RBI-regulated NBFC that securely fetches a borrower’s authenticated bank and other accounts data (like GST returns) to streamline credit assessment. In practice, a borrower can allow a prospective lender to view her bank statements and GST filings via the AA, replacing the need for manual document submission. This enhances underwriting accuracy for cash-flow lending.
bodyText: Under AA rules, banks and NBFCs must obtain explicit consent through the AA network before accessing a customer’s data. For MSMEs, RBI and government agencies are pushing use of GST returns to gauge cash flows. RBI now permits lenders to use GST-tracking (via AAs) as part of their credit appraisal. This is a paradigm shift from collateral-based to data-driven lending: for example, instead of using fixed assets, a bank can underwrite a shop owner’s ₹20 lakh loan by analyzing 6 months of GST invoices and bank inflows via an AA platform. The RBI’s digital lending guidelines implicitly encourage such open data models (as long as privacy is protected). Regulators (RBI, IBBI, GSTN) have jointly built frameworks: GSTN acts as a KYC and data provider (through Accounts Aggregator or NBFC-Factors). Lenders need to verify GSTIN status and utilization to validate turnover. The RBI’s 2022 standards require customer consent and confidentiality for all shared data. Meanwhile, data validation through GST filters out sham businesses. The government’s Unified Lending Interface (ULI) is an upcoming initiative to integrate this: ULI would let a lender fetch customer data (from AAs or government sources) through APIs, assess eligibility and disburse quickly. As of 2026, ULI pilots (e.g. with NBFCs and fintechs) are underway under RBI and IBA supervision. The idea is a one-stop-shop for loan origination: borrower consents once, and multiple lenders can exchange standardized credit data. ### Permanent rule Customer data (bank statements, GST returns, etc.) may be shared with lenders only through RBI-authorised channels (Account Aggregators) and only with customer consent. ### Permanent trap Assuming lenders can scrape GST data directly. In fact, only AAs or designated repositories (with consent) can transmit GST filings to banks. Also, neglecting to update borrower’s risk after changes in their GST activity can misstate credit risk. ### Never confuse **Account Aggregator** — an RBI-regulated data intermediary that moves customer-permissioned data between institutions. --- **GST data** — tax return data of businesses. (Accessible by banks only through AAs or GSTN APIs with consent.) ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — The AA framework is Indian (launched 2021) and unique in mandating customer consent for banking data sharing. No similar centralized data sharing network is in place in UK/US.

title: Open Credit Enablement Network (OCEN) and Unified Lending
one_screen: OCEN is a public digital infrastructure initiated by RBI and others to promote standardized lending processes. It provides open protocols so any bank or NBFC can offer standardized lending products (LOAN service) to any borrower via their preferred interface (called Loan App Provider). The **Unified Lending Interface (ULI)** is an evolution of OCEN – a platform or API layer (conceptualized by IBA/RBI) that allows multiple lenders and tech-entities to interconnect seamlessly for loan origination. In practice, OCEN/ULI aims to let a borrower initiate a loan request once, then multiple lenders can compete or collaborate, all via technology rails.
bodyText: OCEN’s idea: separate *procurement of borrowers* (handled by digital aggregators or apps, called LAPs) from *funding* (banks/NBFCs). Using open APIs (like rupee-instant-pay, AA), a Loan App can share borrower’s data with many lenders using OCEN. Each lender then provides loan quotes. Final loan issuance happens through UPI’s LTI (loan transfer initiation) or direct credit. The OCEN framework is still evolving. It is mandated for certain government loan schemes (like for MSMEs). Under OCEN, lenders must publish their loan “schema” (min criteria) and pricing APIs. Borrowers see an offer comparison screen. Ongoing pilots involve fintech lending apps and major banks. The concept addresses fragmentation – instead of one bank-per-relationship, small borrowers can access many lenders digitally. Regulatory stance: RBI encourages this open network but underscores customer protection (same KFS, consent rules apply). OCEN/ULI bypass middlemen fees and aim for credit deepening. However, RBI has not mandated full roll-out; it’s voluntary with incentives. By 2026 RBI reports many pilots, but wide adoption is pending. Key point: OCEN/ULI are *not* separate entities, just infrastructure standards. ### Permanent rule Forthcoming RBI guideline: digital lenders can use the ULI (under OCEN) to interconnect, but all standard rules (KFS, KYC) still apply. For now, any participation is voluntary but encouraged for efficiency. ### Permanent trap Thinking OCEN/ULI replaces banks. In fact, banks/NBFCs remain the credit providers. OCEN just standardizes the way loan requests flow to them. Another mistake: assuming an app can lend via OCEN without partnering a regulated lender – regulatory approval is still needed. ### Never confuse **OCEN** — a framework of open APIs and data standards for credit enabling (no single “company”). **ULI** — proposed RBI/IBA interface for unified loan origination/decision (still under development). ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — India’s OCEN/ULI initiative is pioneering an open credit network; no identical global standard exists.

title: Credit Information and CIBIL Scores
one_screen: Credit Information Companies (CICs) like CIBIL, Experian, Equifax (licensed by RBI) collect borrowers’ credit data (loans, credit cards, defaults) from banks/NBFCs and provide credit reports and scores. A bureau score (300–900 range) reflects an individual’s or firm’s credit history; lenders use it as a risk indicator. Each loan or card issued is reported to CICs. A CIBIL (now TransUnion CIBIL) *score* is a summary derived from one’s report; though popular, RBI treats it as *one* input, not a sole decision factor.
bodyText: CICs operate under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. By law, any institution granting loans above certain thresholds must report data (including repayment behaviour) to CICs. Thus, a “CIBIL report” may contain: outstanding loans, EMI payment history, credit inquiries, defaults or write-offs. A high credit score (e.g. 750+) typically leads to faster loan approval. However, some segments (like unsecured or newer forms of credit) still rely on alternate data, since CIC coverage has gaps (informal lending not always reported). RBI mandates that lenders consult at least one CIC before sanctioning any loan. Lenders are also regulated on sharing the score with customers (ECIR/ ECI guidelines requiring justification for rejection). Over the past decade, refinements have been made: e.g. CRILC (Central Repository of Information on Large Credits) to flag large defaults, and securitisation of card limits for bureau reporting. Debenture data (various corporate loans) is less visible in consumer credit reports. For corporate or MSME borrowers, there is no single “CIBIL score” standard. Instead, banks rely on financial statements, promoter history, and sometimes the promoter’s personal credit scores. Commercial credit intelligence (like Dun & Bradstreet ratings) complement it. ### Permanent rule Banks and NBFCs must submit borrower data to CICs and use bureau reports in credit decisions. Borrowers have a right to one free credit report per year from each bureau. ### Permanent trap Over-reliance on the numeric score. A common error is to treat a 750 CIBIL score as guarantee of repayment; lenders must still do underwriting. Conversely, a borrower’s poor score may have valid reasons (data errors or past minor defaults) – blindly rejecting such cases without manual review can be wrong. ### Never confuse **Credit report** — detailed history of all borrowed accounts and repays (with any defaults) held by a CIC. **Credit score** — a numerical summary (e.g. CIBIL score) of that report. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — System of multiple CICs (CIBIL, HDFC ERGO, etc.) is similar to US/UK bureau systems. But India’s credit scoring scale (300–900 for CIBIL) is proprietary (others use different ranges).

title: SARFAESI Act (Asset Enforcement)
one_screen: The SARFAESI Act (2002) empowers banks/ARCs to enforce securities against defaulting borrowers without court intervention. It allows a secured creditor (bank/NBFC/ARC) to take possession of collateral (land, factories, financial instruments) if a loan account is an NPA, subject to RBI’s prescribed triggers. This mechanism dramatically speeds up recovery in contrast to civil litigation. However, it only covers “secured” exposures: unsecured debts (like credit cards, personal loans) cannot be directly taken under SARFAESI.
bodyText: Under SARFAESI, upon default, an asset reconstruction company (or the bank itself) can issue a notice to the borrower (and guarantor) demanding payment within 60 days. If not paid, the creditor can auction the pledged assets (e.g. sell the mortgaged factory). The sale proceeds pay off the debt. Borrowers can appeal before DRTs (Debt Recovery Tribunals) if they believe wrongful action. SARFAESI’s enforcement is therefore final, with limited appeals – it is potent. Banks often syndicate bad loans to ARCs (Asset Reconstruction Companies) which use SARFAESI to reorganize or sell assets. For lenders, SARFAESI provides collateral realisation. Practically, banks must follow RBI’s “change of management” norms if a corporate account being taken over exceeds a threshold. RBI also requires lenders to classify any SARFAESI-induced partial recovery appropriately (e.g. as standard if current, else further NPA reduction). In stress scenarios, SARFAESI is often a precursor to invocation of IBC or other legal recovery if needed. ### Permanent rule A secured lender can take possession of pledged collateral if the borrower defaults and does not repay after notice. The process must follow SARFAESI procedures (notice, sale, use funds to settle debt). ### Permanent trap Trying to use SARFAESI on unsecured loans – it only applies to secured advances. Also, failing to issue the proper notice period (60 days) or not following RBI’s change-of-management rules when seizing a company. ### Never confuse **SARFAESI** — enforcement law letting secured creditors seize and sell collateral after default (without courts). **Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)** — quasi-judicial body that borrowers can approach to challenge SARFAESI or other recovery actions. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — Unique to India (introduced 2002). No direct analog in US/UK; other countries rely on normal foreclosure laws.

title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) and DRT
one_screen: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) provides a structured process for resolving stressed corporate debts. If lenders collectively decide (typically 75% by value) that a default requires legal resolution, they can initiate corporate insolvency. A *Resolution Professional* then manages the company’s affairs, and creditors vote on a revival plan. The IBC has priority over SARFAESI in that once an insolvency petition is admitted, SARFAESI proceedings halt. For personal or small debtors, formal bankruptcy via IBC may not apply; instead, DRTs (for bank debts above a threshold) and debt recovery tribunals handle lower-value cases, including unsecured and smaller claims.
bodyText: Under IBC, any financial creditor (bank, NBFC, or even a supplier if admitted) can initiate proceedings when payment default occurs. A strict timeline (330 days max) forces quick action. Successful resolution under IBC often involves structural changes (equity dilution, takeover by new promoters, etc.). Recoveries under IBC have exceeded SARFAESI recoveries historically because of its collective mechanism. But IBC is mostly for corporate debt. For individual/business borrowers, RBI relies on SARFAESI and DRT (established by RDDBFI Act, 1993) and lok adalats. Debt Recovery Tribunals handle all debts of ₹10 lakh and above to banks/financial institutions. They can entertain cases on any credit, secured or not, and can order recovery from a debtor’s assets. There are separate DRTs for circular references from the RBI. The DRT process is formal (like a tribunal court), but faster than regular civil court. DRTs have been strengthened by digital filing and “DRAT” appeals. Banks usually prioritize SARFAESI for quick value, then DRT if borrower defends. IBC is the last resort for viable corporates or when persuasion fails. RBI’s provisions require reclassification of accounts when IBC is filed (they become NPA on petition filing). The IBC can wipe out shareholders; in one instance, leading to EMI refinance rather than further lending. ### Permanent rule Under IBC, when a corporate borrower defaults, lenders may trigger insolvency proceedings with RBI filing specified asset classification. DRTs handle recovery suits for any loan above ₹10 lakh. ### Permanent trap Missing the priority: initiating SARFAESI on a company after IBC has been filed – not allowed, since IBC is a binding multilateral process once admitted. Also, dismissing smaller claims (below 10 lakh) thinking only big debts go to DRTs – DRT jurisdiction starts at ₹10 lakh for banks. ### Never confuse **IBC (Corporate)** — structured insolvency process for companies / FIs (time-bound, collective). **DRT (Debt Recovery)** — tribunal for creditor claims on individuals or businesses (₹10L+), including enforcement of guarantee by guarantors. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — The IBC is India’s consolidated insolvency law (2016). Countries like the UK/US have different corporate insolvency regimes (Chapter 11, administration, etc.), but the IBC’s speed and creditor primacy are quite distinctive.

title: Fair Practices Code and Rate Transparency
one_screen: RBI mandates all banks/NBFCs adopt a *Fair Practices Code (FPC)* – a set of consumer-lending norms. The FPC requires clear, upfront disclosure of key loan terms (interest rates, all fees, prepayment and foreclosure conditions). Borrowers must receive written sanction letters. Lenders must not coerce borrowers into purchasing unrelated products. After 2019, RBI additionally requires all new floating-rate loans (e.g. mortgages, auto loans, corporate loans) to be linked to external benchmarks (like RBI’s repo rate or govt bond yields). This makes the rate formula transparent – borrowers know that if RBI changes repo, their EMI changes per a public index.
bodyText: For instance, every home loan borrower must be told the benchmark (now MCLR or an external rate) and margin. Any change in the base rate must be communicated one month in advance. Prepayment or foreclosure should be allowed per the FPC (sometimes with max 2% penalty). No hidden charges are allowed. If a bank refuses to lend, it must give a reason in writing (borrower’s right to information under FPC). The 2019 “external benchmark” circular mandated that by Oct 1, 2019 all new floating-rate personal, retail, and MSME loans link to external benchmarks, and from April 1, 2020 medium enterprise loans too. This revolutionized rate transparency: borrowers now see explicit linkage to, say, RBI’s repo. Banks cannot arbitrarily change rates without a rule. In essence, fair practices and rate guidelines aim to protect retail borrowers from predatory pricing and information asymmetry. While bankers often resent caps on lending rates, RBI views transparency (e.g. bench-marking) as non-negotiable. All retail credit product literature (e.g. home loans, auto, personal loans) must clearly detail these terms. ### Permanent rule Lenders must disclose all loan terms in writing (sanction letter or KFS) per RBI’s FPC. All new floating-rate loans must use an external benchmark (e.g. policy rate) for interest calculations. ### Permanent trap Failing to update borrowers on rate changes. RBI requires communication if the external benchmark shifts. Some banks adjust rates silently (not allowed). Also, bundling hidden fees into loan rate rather than showing them separately violates FPC. ### Never confuse **Fair Practices Code (FPC)** — RBI’s consumer protection rules for lending (disclosure, no coercion, grievance mechanism). **External Benchmarking** — the requirement that floating rates link to public indices. This is part of FPC transparency. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s mandatory external benchmark linkage (repo or gilt) is specific to India’s circulars. Elsewhere, countries may require APR disclosure but not compulsory benchmark linking.

title: Recovery Agents Code of Conduct
one_screen: RBI’s 2022 guidelines reaffirm that financial institutions are fully responsible for their recovery agents’ actions. Banks must ensure recovery personnel treat borrowers respectfully, within prescribed hours, and without intimidation. Agents must carry ID cards. Borrowers can record collection calls and lodge complaints if the code is violated. This rule curbs the excesses of aggressive recovery practices prevalent especially in rural/tele-calling.
bodyText: The key directives (2022) state that banks/NBFCs must not use agents to harass borrowers. No coercion is allowed: no making calls before 8 am or after 7 pm, no abuse/insults, no shame-tactics. Agents must have clear ID/name tags; they must follow written guidelines. The regulated entity (bank or NBFC) remains liable for any breach by its agents. Prior RBI codes (2006 & 2010) prohibited many misbehaviors (e.g. third-party visits to workplaces for small debts). The 2022 circular specifically supplements these with updated instructions under the outsourcing framework, emphasizing that violations can lead to supervisory action. This is consumer protection in collections: borrowers have recourse to the bank’s grievance cell for any agent mis-step, and ultimately to the Ombudsman. Banks must train and monitor their agents (even if they are third-party contractors). ### Permanent rule Banks/NBFCs must ensure recovery agents comply with RBI’s conduct rules: no threat, no personal harassment, call only between 8am-7pm, respectful behavior. ID cards are mandatory. ### Permanent trap Assuming recovery can be “any means necessary.” RBI’s explicit code bans intimidation (Verbal/physical harassment, false claims, repeated late-hour calls). Non-compliance by agents is deemed violation by the lender. ### Never confuse **Recovery Agent** — hired agent or third-party who collects overdue loans. (Subject to RBI’s code of conduct.) **Debt Collector** — similar role; RBI’s rules apply equivalently, unlike unregulated field agents for non-financial debts. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s Code for recovery agents is detailed and mandatory (2016/2022). Other countries regulate debt collectors (e.g. US Fair Debt Collection Practices Act) differently, but India’s code is specific to banking debts.

title: What Counts as a Model
one_screen: A model is a governed representation that transforms inputs into outputs using assumptions and quantitative or cognitive techniques. Classification is consequential: model status brings inventory, validation, approval, monitoring and change controls, while the legal boundary differs materially across jurisdictions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Test | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Inputs | Does it consume data, estimates, judgement or structured inputs? | | Transformation | Does it apply statistical, mathematical, economic, financial or comparable analytical assumptions or techniques? | | Output | Does it estimate, predict, classify, rank, optimise or inform a decision? | | Uncertainty | Can data, assumptions or method make the output wrong even when implementation is correct? | | Use | Does output affect business, risk, reporting, capital, customer or operational decisions? | Model classification follows substance, not software: ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Tool/model owner | Proposes classification and documents function and use | | MRM function | Challenges boundary decisions | | Business user | Identifies actual decision impact | | Internal audit | Tests classification controls | ### Permanent rule Classify the method and its use, not its technology label. "Spreadsheet", "algorithm" and "AI" do not determine model status by themselves. ### Never confuse [Model] and [Non-model tool] **Model** - uses assumptions and analytical techniques to transform inputs into estimates or decision-relevant outputs with model uncertainty. --- **Non-model tool** - performs deterministic processing without the model characteristics defined by the applicable framework, though it can still require strong controls. ### Permanent trap Treating "not a model" as "not risky". A material deterministic calculator can cause major loss even when legitimately outside the model inventory. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Definition / scope | Boundary / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2: complex quantitative method using statistical/economic/financial theories on inputs for estimates. | Simple arithmetic/deterministic rules without those theories excluded. | | UK | SS1/23: quantitative methods using statistical/economic/financial/mathematical theories, techniques and assumptions. | Broader; material complex deterministic methods outside scope may still warrant MRM controls. | | EU | ECB Guide: CRR internal models. | No enterprise-wide definition. | | IN | Draft: broad input-processing-output test including internal/third-party/AI/ML systems. | Draft as at August 2026; issued 24 June 2026; consultation closed 24 July 2026. |

title: Model Risk as a Distinct Risk Type
one_screen: Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from relying on a model whose design, data, implementation, limitations or use make its output unreliable for the decision being taken. It is distinct from the underlying risk being measured: the borrower can be unchanged while a credit model is wrong, and the market can be unchanged while a valuation model is wrong.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What can go wrong | | :--- | :--- | | Underlying credit exposure | Borrower fails to pay | | Market position | Prices or rates move adversely | | Liquidity position | Cash cannot be raised when needed | | Model | The institution measures, predicts or acts on those risks incorrectly | A model can be technically sound yet still generate model risk if it is used outside its intended population, horizon or decision context. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Identifies and manages model-specific risk | | Business user | Understands limitations before consuming output | | MRM / validation | Independently challenges reliability and use | | Senior management | Oversees material model risk within appetite | ### Permanent rule Model risk belongs to the use of the representation, not to the underlying exposure itself. ### Never confuse [Model risk] and [Underlying financial risk] **Model risk** - risk that reliance on a model contributes to an adverse decision or outcome. --- **Underlying financial risk** - risk inherent in the exposure or activity being modelled, such as borrower default, market movement or funding stress. ### Permanent trap Explaining an unexpected loss entirely as "credit risk" or "market risk" without asking whether the model mismeasured the risk, was used outside scope or produced misleading outputs. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The cited frameworks differ in perimeter and prescription, but all treat model risk as a risk arising from model use rather than as another name for the risk the model measures.

title: Where Model Risk Comes From
one_screen: Model risk is rarely one defect called "bad modelling". It can enter through data, assumptions, methodology, implementation, use or environmental change, and the same bad output can require a completely different remedy depending on which source failed.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Source | Failure mode | Typical control response | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Data | Wrong, incomplete, biased, stale or unrepresentative inputs | Repair lineage, quality or sampling | | Assumptions | Simplifications cease to hold | Challenge, constrain or revise assumptions | | Methodology | Model form does not represent the problem adequately | Redesign or redevelop | | Implementation | Code, configuration or interface differs from approved design | Correct implementation and retest | | Use | Output is misinterpreted or applied outside intended scope | Restrict use, train users, reapprove | | Environment | Population, behaviour or relationships change | Monitor, recalibrate or redevelop | | Governance | Weak challenge allows known limitations to persist | Escalate, remediate, strengthen control | The categories can interact: Data shift → assumption no longer holds → calibration deteriorates → users apply stale output → losses increase Root-cause analysis therefore matters more than attaching a generic "model underperformance" label. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Developer / owner | Controls design, data and implementation risks | | Model user | Controls scope, interpretation and use risk | | MRM / validation | Challenges all sources and their interactions | | Internal audit | Assesses whether the control framework catches them | ### Permanent rule A performance symptom is not a root cause. Diagnose where the failure entered before choosing the remedy. ### Never confuse [Implementation error] and [Model limitation] **Implementation error** - the production system does not execute the approved model correctly. --- **Model limitation** - the approved model itself has a known boundary, approximation or uncertainty even when implemented exactly as designed. ### Permanent trap Responding to every poor result with recalibration. Recalibration may repair stale parameter levels; it does not fix corrupted data, bad code, conceptual misspecification or misuse. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. Data, design, implementation, use and environmental change are universal sources even though regulators express them with different terminology.

title: The Regulatory Perimeter: US, UK, EU and India
one_screen: There is no single global legal perimeter for MRM. The US uses broad, tailored supervisory guidance; the PRA applies SS1/23 to specified firms but across their model types; the EU prudential regime focuses on approved internal models; and India's proposed 2026 framework is broader but remains draft as at August 2026.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Jurisdiction | Institution perimeter | Model perimeter | August 2026 status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Most relevant above USD 30bn; possible relevance below where model risk is significant | Traditional quantitative and qualifying non-generative, non-agentic AI models | Live supervisory guidance | | UK | Specified PRA firms with internal model approval | SS1/23 principles across model and risk types in those firms | Live supervisory statement | | EU | CRR institutions using permitted internal approaches | Internal credit, market and counterparty credit risk models | Live prudential framework | | IN | Eleven proposed categories of RBI-regulated entities | All models, including third-party and AI/ML | Draft; consultation closed | Entity → applicable instrument → model population → control obligations A bank may voluntarily govern more models than the legal minimum. That policy choice does not make the regulatory perimeters identical. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Separate three questions: "Is this a model?", "Is this institution in scope?", and "Does this instrument apply?" A yes to one does not answer the others. ### Permanent trap Importing one jurisdiction's requirement into another and presenting it as universal. Scope and prescription genuinely differ here. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Scope | Status / delta | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | SR 26-2/OCC Bulletin 2026-13; most relevant above USD 30bn, potentially below where model risk is significant. | Issued 17 April 2026; replaced 2011 guidance; risk-based, non-prescriptive. | | UK | Specified PRA firms with internal-model approval; new permission gives 12 months to comply; principles extend beyond approved capital models. | Current SS1/23 effective 23 April 2026. | | EU | ECB Guide covers approved CRR internal models. | Revised 28 July 2025; supervisory CRR interpretation, not enterprise MRM code. | | IN | Proposed regulatory MRM framework. | Draft as at August 2026; issued 24 June 2026; comments closed 24 July 2026; placeholder circular number invalid. |

title: Model Inventory and Dependency Map
one_screen: The model inventory is the authoritative record of what models exist, where they are in the lifecycle, who owns and uses them, and which other systems or models they depend on. A mere list of names is insufficient: the control value comes from linking identity, status, use, lineage, dependencies and governance state.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Inventory field | Control question | | :--- | :--- | | Model ID/version | Exact governed object? | | Purpose/use | Which decision depends on it? | | Owner/user | Who is accountable/consumes output? | | Risk tier | Required control intensity? | | Status | Development, validation, active, restricted, inactive or retired? | | Validation/approval | Authorised, with what conditions? | | Upstream dependencies | What can contaminate it? | | Downstream consumers | What fails if it fails? | | Third-party status | External dependency? | | Limitations/issues | Known open weaknesses? | Model A data → Model B estimate → Model C decision output Dependency mapping links inventory rows into chains, exposing propagation when upstream failure contaminates downstream models. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Keeps model record accurate | | Business / technology | Confirms actual use and dependencies | | MRM function | Sets inventory standards and challenges completeness | | Internal audit | Tests completeness and reconciliation | ### Permanent rule One model has one governed identity, but it may have many uses, versions and dependencies. Inventory controls must preserve that distinction. ### Never confuse [Model inventory] and [Model repository] **Model inventory** - authoritative governance record showing models, status, ownership and control attributes. --- **Model repository** - storage location for code, documentation, artefacts or files; it may support the inventory but does not replace it. ### Permanent trap Keeping retired or restricted models invisible. Historical lineage matters for reproducing past decisions, understanding inherited outputs and managing transitions. ### Jurisdiction variants | Jurisdiction | Inventory expectation | Scope / status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | US | Risk-based identification sufficient for individual and aggregate model-risk oversight; no fixed template. | 2026 guidance less prescriptive than predecessor. | | UK | SS1/23 Principle 1: identify models, maintain inventory, classify risk for proportionate controls. | Formal inventory expectation. | | EU | CRR/ECB governs prudential model scope, rating systems, changes and permissions. | No enterprise inventory mandate for every quantitative tool. | | IN | Proposed current inventory covering active, inactive, decommissioned, third-party and AI/ML models. | Draft as at August 2026; not final. |

title: Materiality and Risk Tiering
one_screen: Tiering converts model characteristics and business impact into proportional control intensity. The purpose is not to declare low-tier models harmless; it is to spend validation, approval, monitoring and governance effort where model failure can matter most while preserving a minimum control floor for every governed model.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Driver | What it captures | | :--- | :--- | | Inherent risk | Complexity, assumptions, input quality, data constraints | | Purpose | Importance of the decision or regulatory use | | Exposure | Scale of balances, customers, transactions or business affected | | Materiality | Significance of purpose plus exposure | | Consumer / operational impact | Harm beyond direct financial exposure | | Changeability | Dynamic behaviour or frequent updating | | Dependency | Whether other important models rely on it | A simple model can be high risk because its output affects a huge portfolio. A complex model can be lower materiality if it has narrow, non-critical use. Complexity and materiality therefore answer different questions. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Tiering scales controls; it never removes accountability. A lower tier means proportionate MRM, not exemption from all governance. ### Never confuse [Complexity] and [Materiality] **Complexity** - difficulty of understanding, estimating, implementing or challenging the model. --- **Materiality** - significance of the model's output to decisions and exposures. A model can be simple but highly material. ### Permanent trap Building a score that lets one benign factor cancel a critical one. A highly material model should not become "low risk" merely because its technique is simple. ### Jurisdiction variants #### US (Federal Reserve / OCC) SR 26-2 distinguishes inherent risk, model exposure and model purpose. Purpose together with exposure determines materiality; overall model risk reflects inherent risk in the context of materiality. Higher materiality warrants more rigorous oversight, while immaterial models may receive more limited controls. #### UK (PRA) SS1/23 expects firms to classify model risk and use proportionality so the level of MRM activity reflects the model's risk. The PRA does not require every firm to use the same numerical tiering scale. #### IN (RBI) As at August 2026, the RBI draft proposes risk-based tiering for all models, with materiality, complexity and other relevant factors considered collectively. The proposed tier drives validation, approval, monitoring, reporting and business-continuity intensity; high-risk models receive stronger governance. It remains draft.

title: Aggregate Model Risk and Risk Appetite
one_screen: Managing models one by one can miss the largest exposure: several individually acceptable models may rely on the same data, assumptions, vendor or economic relationship and fail together. Aggregate model risk therefore combines model-level risk with concentration and dependency, then compares that enterprise exposure with the institution's model risk appetite and tolerance.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Aggregation lens | Example question | | :--- | :--- | | Common data | How many models depend on the same customer master or market feed? | | Common methodology | Would one invalid assumption impair several models? | | Model chains | Does an upstream output feed many downstream decisions? | | Vendor concentration | Could one provider outage or defect affect many models? | | Business concentration | Are critical decisions clustered around a small model set? | | Technology concentration | Do several models share one platform or implementation layer? | Risk appetite states how much model risk the institution is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance converts that high-level appetite into actionable boundaries, escalation triggers or control expectations. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owners | Report model-level risk and dependencies | | Enterprise MRM | Aggregates risk and identifies concentration | | Senior management | Operates within approved appetite | | Board / relevant committee | Oversees appetite and material breaches | ### Permanent rule Portfolio diversification of financial exposures does not guarantee diversification of model risk. Shared models, data and assumptions can create hidden common-mode failure. ### Never confuse [Model tier] and [Model risk appetite] **Model tier** - classification of one model used to scale its controls. --- **Model risk appetite** - enterprise statement of how much model risk the institution is prepared to accept and under what constraints. ### Permanent trap Adding model risk scores as though they were independent. Aggregation must recognise dependencies and correlated failure, not just arithmetic totals. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The exact appetite framework is institution-specific, but assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate and governing material exposures is a common MRM principle.

title: The Model Lifecycle and Its Control Gates
one_screen: A model lifecycle is not a project plan; it is a sequence of governed states in which evidence must be sufficient before the model can move forward. The key control idea is the gate: development does not grant use, validation does not grant approval, approval does not end monitoring, and change can reopen earlier gates.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Gate | Minimum decision | | :--- | :--- | | Development complete | Is the evidence pack sufficient for independent challenge? | | Validation complete | Is the model reliable enough for its intended use, with known limitations? | | Approval | Is residual model risk acceptable and use authorised? | | Deployment | Does production reproduce the approved model? | | Monitoring | Does evidence still support continued use? | | Change | Does the change reopen validation or approval? | | Retirement | Can use cease without breaking dependencies or records? | Lifecycle controls are recursive. A material change can return an active model to development, validation and approval rather than allowing an informal production patch. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Model owner | Coordinates the model through lifecycle stages | | Developer | Produces development and change evidence | | Validation / MRM | Independently challenges relevant stages | | Approval authority | Authorises use and material changes | | Business user | Operates only within approved conditions | ### Permanent rule A lifecycle stage creates evidence; a gate creates authority. Evidence from one stage is not authority to skip the next. ### Never confuse [Validation] and [Approval] **Validation** - independent assessment of reliability, limitations and fitness for intended use. --- **Approval** - governance decision to accept residual risk and authorise specified use, possibly with conditions. ### Permanent trap Treating "live" as the final state. Production use begins a new control phase in which monitoring, issue management, change and eventual retirement remain governed. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta. The cited regimes use different language and degrees of prescription, but the lifecycle logic of development, challenge, approval, use, monitoring, change and exit is common.

title: Who Produces, Uses, Approves, Challenges and Audits
one_screen: Ownership is the load-bearing control in MRM because the same person should not create evidence, decide whether that evidence is convincing, accept the residual risk and audit the process.
